explanation: Because of the bends and turns in coils and curls, the natural oils from the scalp have a harder time sliding down the full length of the hair. [learn more](GNS112_U5_T5#GNS112_U5_T5_h4)

question: A bedridden patient has severely matted hair after weeks of illness. What should you do first?

options.A: Ignore the matting until the patient is fully discharged from the hospital
options.B: Wash the hair with a harsh clarifying shampoo to break apart the tangles
options.C: Cut the matted sections off immediately to save time during the bed bath
options.D: Apply a conditioner or detangling spray and work through small sections with a wide-toothed comb

explanation: Always respect your patient's dignity. Working gently with a lubricant and a wide-toothed comb avoids painful pulling and protects their personal autonomy. [learn more](GNS112_U5_T5#GNS112_U5_T5_h4)

question: What are the tiny eggs of head lice that attach firmly to the hair shaft called?

options.A: Nits
options.B: Larvae
options.C: Spores
options.D: Pustules

explanation: Nits are the tiny, oval eggs that head lice cement securely onto individual strands of hair. [learn more](GNS112_U5_T5#GNS112_U5_T5_h5)

question: Why do fungal scalp infections like ringworm (tinea capitis) usually need oral medication instead of just medicated shampoo?

options.A: Shampoos cannot easily penetrate deep into the hair follicle where the fungus lives
options.B: Oral medications are cheaper and easier for hospitalized patients to swallow
options.C: Medicated shampoos will permanently damage the texture of the hair shaft
options.D: Fungal infections on the head are completely unaffected by topical treatments

explanation: Washing the surface isn't always enough because the fungus digs deep inside the hair follicle where shampoos can't easily reach. [learn more](GNS112_U5_T5#GNS112_U5_T5_h5)

question: Which detail is most important to include in your notes when charting routine hair care?

options.A: The exact minute the hair drying process started
options.B: Condition of the scalp and any abnormal findings
options.C: The total cost of the hair care products used
options.D: The exact brand of shampoo preferred by the nurse

explanation: Always focus your documentation on clear clinical facts, such as how the scalp looks and any unusual signs you spot. [learn more](GNS112_U5_T5#GNS112_U5_T5_h6)

question: What is the main goal of teaching a family home care after treating a patient for head lice?

options.A: To prove that the nursing staff performed their duties correctly
options.B: To prevent reinfection and spread among household members
options.C: To force the family to cut their hair short for safety
options.D: To ensure the patient buys the most expensive commercial products

explanation: Good teaching helps families clean bedding and check everyone else, stopping the lice from spreading right back to the patient! [learn more](GNS112_U5_T5#GNS112_U5_T5_h6)

question: What is the primary cause of tissue damage in a pressure sore?

options.A: Prolonged pressure cutting off blood supply
options.B: Excessive moisture from heavy sweating
options.C: Bacterial infection of the sweat glands
options.D: Allergic reaction to hospital bedsheets

explanation: Pressure sores form when constant external pressure stops blood flow to the skin and deep tissues, causing them to die from lack of oxygen. [learn more](GNS112_U5_T6#GNS112_U5_T6_h1)

question: Why do deep tissues near the bone often get damaged before the outer skin shows a break?

options.A: Deep muscle and fat layers need oxygen more and are weaker against lack of blood flow than surface skin.
options.B: Bacterial growth starts deep inside the bone marrow.
options.C: Outer skin has a natural defense system that completely blocks pressure.
options.D: Sweat and moisture accumulate underneath the skin layers first.

explanation: Think of deep tissues like hungry muscles near the bone—they need lots of oxygen and give out much faster when blood supply is blocked, even before the outer skin looks broken! [learn more](GNS112_U5_T6#GNS112_U5_T6_h1)

question: Which bony area is at the highest risk for pressure sores when a patient lies flat on their back?

options.A: Collarbone
options.B: Forehead
options.C: Kneecap
options.D: Sacrum

explanation: The sacrum bears a large amount of body weight when a patient is in the supine position, making it a primary site for pressure sores. [learn more](GNS112_U5_T6#GNS112_U5_T6_h2)

question: A patient sitting in a wheelchair for long hours is most likely to develop pressure sores on which specific area?

options.A: Ischial tuberosities
options.B: Occipital bone
options.C: Bridge of the nose
options.D: Anterior patella

explanation: The ischial tuberosities are simply your sitting bones! When a patient sits for too long, these bones take the heavy brunt of the body weight. [learn more](GNS112_U5_T6#GNS112_U5_T6_h2)

question: What is the main difference between shear and friction in skin breakdown?

options.A: Shear only happens on the heels, whereas friction only happens on the sacrum.
options.B: Shear happens when bones slide inside while skin stays stuck; friction is just surface rubbing.
options.C: Shear damages bone tissue, whereas friction only damages hair follicles.
options.D: Shear is caused by moisture, whereas friction is caused by lack of protein.

explanation: Friction is like skin rubbing against bedsheets, but shear happens when the skeleton slides down while the outer skin stays put, twisting the blood vessels inside. You've got this! [learn more](GNS112_U5_T6#GNS112_U5_T6_h3)

question: Which nutritional deficiency significantly increases a patient's risk of getting pressure sores?

options.A: Protein deficiency
options.B: Sodium overload
options.C: Vitamin C excess
options.D: Carbohydrate restriction

explanation: Protein is like the building blocks for healthy skin. Without enough protein, the skin becomes weak, fragile, and takes forever to repair itself! [learn more](GNS112_U5_T6#GNS112_U5_T6_h3)

question: How is a Stage 1 pressure sore best identified on light-skinned patients?

options.A: Intact skin with redness that does not turn white when pressed
options.B: An open crater exposing subcutaneous fat and muscle
options.C: A black, hard scab covering deep tissue damage
options.D: A shallow pink wound with clear fluid drainage

explanation: In Stage 1, the skin isn't broken yet, but it shows redness that stays red even when you press a finger on it (non-blanching). Good to know for your ward rotations! [learn more](GNS112_U5_T6#GNS112_U5_T6_h4)

question: Why is a pressure ulcer sometimes classified as 'unstageable'?

options.A: Thick dead tissue or scabs cover the base, hiding the actual depth of the wound.
options.B: It has equal characteristics of both Stage 1 and Stage 4 simultaneously.
options.C: The patient is moving around too much during the assessment.
options.D: The wound is healing too fast to determine its exact category.

explanation: If stubborn yellow, brown, or black dead tissue blocks your view, you can't see how deep the wound actually goes. Once that's cleared, you can finally stage it properly! [learn more](GNS112_U5_T6#GNS112_U5_T6_h4)

question: A patient has a pressure sore with a thick layer of black dead tissue covering the base. What action is needed first for effective healing?

options.A: Applying dry gauze directly over the black tissue
options.B: Debridement to remove the dead tissue
options.C: Immediate closure with skin grafts without cleaning
options.D: Soaking the entire wound in hydrogen peroxide daily

explanation: That black dead tissue (eschar) acts like a shield trapping bacteria and blocking new growth. It has to be safely cleared away (debrided) before healing can truly begin. [learn more](GNS112_U5_T6#GNS112_U5_T6_h5)

question: What is the standard rule for turning a bed-bound patient to help prevent pressure sores?

options.A: Every two hours
options.B: Every six hours
options.C: Once per shift
options.D: Only when they complain of pain

explanation: Turning a patient at least every two hours takes the weight off vulnerable spots, giving blood flow a chance to rush back in and save the skin. Simple and life-saving! [learn more](GNS112_U5_T6#GNS112_U5_T6_h6)

question: Which tool is commonly used by nurses to check a patient's risk of developing pressure sores upon admission?

options.A: Apgar Score
options.B: Glasgow Coma Scale
options.C: Braden Scale
options.D: Pain Numeric Rating Scale

explanation: The Braden Scale is your go-to clinical tool! It checks things like moisture, mobility, and nutrition to give you a clear score of a patient's pressure sore risk. [learn more](GNS112_U5_T6#GNS112_U5_T6_h6)

question: What is the medical term for difficulty swallowing?

options.A: Deglutition
options.B: Aspiration
options.C: Dysphagia
options.D: Peristalsis

explanation: Dysphagia is the clinical term used when a patient experiences trouble moving food or liquid from the mouth to the stomach safely. [learn more](GNS112_U5_T7#GNS112_U5_T7_h1)

question: Which little flap of tissue automatically covers your windpipe when you swallow, keeping food out of your lungs?

options.A: The epiglottis
options.B: The uvula
options.C: The lower esophageal sphincter
options.D: The soft palate

explanation: Think of the epiglottis as a trapdoor! When you swallow, it folds down over your larynx and trachea to block food and drinks from taking a wrong turn into your lungs.

question: What is the main danger when food or liquid silently slips into a patient's lungs without them even coughing?

options.A: Development of aspiration pneumonia
options.B: Immediate complete upper airway blockage
options.C: Rapid electrolyte imbalance and dehydration
options.D: Sudden severe allergic skin rashes

explanation: When foreign material and mouth bacteria sneak down into the lungs, they set up camp and cause a nasty infection known as aspiration pneumonia. Always stay alert!

question: Your patient just took a sip of water and now sounds wet and gurgling when they speak. What is your very first nursing move?

options.A: Document normal finding and continue the meal
options.B: Stop feeding immediately and assess the airway
options.C: Encourage the patient to talk more to clear the voice
options.D: Offer a thicker fluid to clear the throat

explanation: That wet voice is a red flag telling you liquid has hit the vocal cords! Stop the meal right away to protect your patient from choking or lung infections.

question: What is the best bed position to set a patient in before you feed them?

options.A: 45 degrees
options.B: 90 degrees
options.C: 30 degrees
options.D: 15 degrees

explanation: Sitting them straight up (High Fowler's at 90 degrees) lets gravity do the hard work, pulling food safely down the esophagus instead of toward the airway.

question: Why should you keep a patient sitting upright for about 30 to 60 minutes after they finish eating?

options.A: To encourage active digestion and prevent constipation
options.B: To prevent gastric reflux and subsequent aspiration
options.C: To allow the nurse time to chart the intake accurately
options.D: To improve nutrient absorption in the small intestine

explanation: Gravity is your best friend here! Keeping them upright stops food and stomach acid from creeping back up into the throat while digestion gets started.

question: How does tucking the chin down to the chest help a patient who has trouble swallowing?

options.A: It narrows the airway entrance to protect the lungs
options.B: It relaxes the jaw muscles during heavy chewing
options.C: It opens the lower esophageal sphincter faster
options.D: It increases saliva production in the oral cavity

explanation: The chin-tuck is a neat trick! It physically shifts the throat structures to close off the windpipe, giving food a safer path to the stomach.

question: You are feeding a patient who looks very tired and worn out. What is the safest way to handle their meal?

options.A: Allowing frequent rest periods and offering smaller, more frequent meals
options.B: Laying the patient flat in bed to conserve their physical energy
options.C: Mixing all the food together so it is easier to swallow quickly
options.D: Feeding the remaining food much faster to finish on time

explanation: Tired muscles make swallowing mistakes easy. Pacing the meal and serving smaller portions keeps your patient safe and energized.

question: Which food texture is safest for a patient with severe swallowing difficulties and missing teeth?

options.A: Regular solid
options.B: Raw vegetables
options.C: Pureed
options.D: Mechanically soft

explanation: Pureed foods are smooth and need zero chewing effort, making them much safer and easier for a struggling patient to swallow.

question: Why do speech therapists and nurses sometimes add thickeners to drinks for dysphagia patients?

options.A: They slow down the flow rate to allow airway closure time
options.B: They prevent the liquid from tasting bitter to the patient
options.C: They provide extra calories and protein for wound healing
options.D: They stimulate the taste buds to increase appetite

explanation: Thin liquids rush down a weak throat way too fast before the epiglottis can close. Thickening the drink slows it down just enough for a safe swallow!

question: What is an important nursing task to do right after a patient finishes eating to lower their risk of pneumonia?

options.A: Encouraging immediate strenuous walking
options.B: Lowering the head of the bed completely
options.C: Offering a large glass of thin water
options.D: Providing thorough oral hygiene

explanation: Brushing the teeth and cleaning the mouth clears away leftover food bits and bacteria that could otherwise slip into the lungs later.

question: Why is it smart to check inside a patient's mouth with a penlight after they finish a meal?

options.A: To check for leftover food pockets that could lead to aspiration
options.B: To ensure the patient has brushed their own teeth properly
options.C: To check if the patient's dentures need permanent resizing
options.D: To measure the exact pH of the remaining saliva

explanation: Patients with weak mouth muscles often hoard food in their cheeks. Finding and clearing those pockets prevents food from sliding into the airway later!

question: Why would a nurse need to provide alternative ways for a patient to pass urine or stool?

options.A: The patient is unable to walk to the toilet independently
options.B: The hospital policy requires all bedridden patients to use bedpans
options.C: It reduces the total amount of daily nursing documentation
options.D: It completely prevents any risk of a hospital-acquired infection

explanation: You've got this! We bring in things like bedpans or urinals mainly when a patient is too weak or restricted to safely make it to the bathroom on their own. Simple and practical!

question: Why should you check a patient's normal bathroom habits before handing them a bedpan or urinal?

options.A: It proves whether the hospital kitchen is providing the right meals
options.B: It prevents the patient from ever needing a catheter later on
options.C: It helps match the intervention to the patient's habits and preserves dignity
options.D: It tells the doctor exactly when to discharge the patient home

explanation: Great nursing is all about respect and personal touch. Knowing when your patient usually goes helps you offer help at the right time, easing their anxiety and keeping their dignity intact.

question: Which type of bedpan is best to use for a patient who has a broken hip?

options.A: A standard high-backed bedpan
options.B: A rigid plastic commode chair
options.C: A fracture pan
options.D: A pediatric incontinence ring

explanation: Fracture pans are shallow, meaning you don't have to lift the patient's hips high up. This is a lifesaver for avoiding extra pain or injury when dealing with hip or pelvic bones!

question: Your patient cannot lift their hips off the bed to get a bedpan underneath. What is the safest way to help them?

options.A: Raise the head of the bed to the high Fowler position before sliding the pan downward
options.B: Forcefully slide the standard bedpan underneath the patient using maximum pulling force
options.C: Leave the patient without a bedpan until a doctor writes a specific order to lift them
options.D: Roll the patient onto their side, place the bedpan against the buttocks, and roll them back

explanation: Never force equipment under a patient! Rolling them gently onto a properly placed pan protects their delicate skin from friction and painful shearing forces.

question: What is the main use of a urinal in the ward?

options.A: To collect stool samples from patients with gastrointestinal bleeding
options.B: To measure precise fluid intake during intravenous therapy
options.C: To collect urine from male patients who cannot walk to the bathroom
options.D: To replace indwelling urinary catheters in surgical patients permanently

explanation: Urinals are shaped specially for male anatomy so patients who are stuck in bed can pass urine easily without fuss. You will see these all the time on the medical-surgical wards!

question: Why is it important to empty and wash a urinal right after a patient uses it?

options.A: It is required before the patient is allowed to drink more water
options.B: It prevents accidental spills and unpleasant odors in the patient room
options.C: It ensures the plastic material does not melt near the bed
options.D: It stops the patient from producing too much urine overnight

explanation: Leaving a full urinal around is an accident waiting to happen—plus, nobody wants a smelly ward room! Prompt clearing keeps the environment fresh and safe.

question: What is one of the biggest dangers of leaving a patient in a wet or soiled adult diaper for too long?

options.A: Permanent kidney failure
options.B: Skin breakdown and pressure injury
options.C: Chronic high blood pressure
options.D: Sudden loss of upper body strength

explanation: Moisture and waste trap heat and wetness against the skin, breaking down its defenses fast. Keeping patients clean and dry is one of your core superpowers as a nurse!

question: When is the right time to change an absorbent diaper or pad for your patient?

options.A: Right before the doctor arrives for ward round
options.B: As soon as the patient complains of feeling hungry
options.C: Promptly whenever it becomes soiled or wet
options.D: Only once every twenty-four hours during the morning shift

explanation: Don't wait for a schedule if comfort and skin health are on the line. Check frequently and change diapers right away when they are wet or soiled.

question: When giving perineal care, in which direction should you wash to prevent spreading germs?

options.A: From the rectum toward the urethral meatus
options.B: From side to side across the pubic bone
options.C: In a circular motion starting from the outer thighs inward
options.D: From the urethral meatus toward the rectum

explanation: Always think 'front to back'! Wiping from the urinary opening toward the back keeps nasty bowel bacteria away from the urinary tract, preventing painful UTIs.

question: Why is patting the perineal skin dry just as important as washing it?

options.A: Wet skin makes it impossible to apply a clean hospital gown
options.B: Leaving moisture behind fosters bacterial growth and skin breakdown
options.C: Rough rubbing removes the patient's natural body hair
options.D: Moisture attracts insects into the hospital room

explanation: Germs love warm, wet places. Taking that extra second to pat the area completely dry is a simple step that keeps skin strong and healthy.

question: Which of these actions breaks basic infection control rules during elimination care?

options.A: Wearing clean gloves while emptying a urine collection container
options.B: Placing a used bedpan on the patient's overbed table
options.C: Keeping the call bell within reach of the patient
options.D: Washing hands before and after providing perineal care

explanation: Yikes! Overbed tables are meant for clean things like food and drinks. Putting a dirty bedpan there spreads germs where people eat.

question: Why is keeping the call bell right next to the patient so important for safe bathroom care?

options.A: It controls the room lighting and temperature automatically
options.B: It allows the patient to call for help before attempting risky, unassisted bathroom trips
options.C: It stops the patient from ever needing a bedpan during the night shift
options.D: It ensures the nurse can check the patient's telephone messages quickly

explanation: A reachable call bell is a fall-prevention tool! It reminds patients they don't have to struggle alone and encourages them to call you instead of risking a dangerous fall.

question: What is the main goal of environmental hygiene in public health?

options.A: Curing chronic illnesses using modern hospital equipment
options.B: Preventing diseases by controlling harmful environmental factors
options.C: Improving agricultural crop production and food storage
options.D: Increasing the economic wealth of local communities

explanation: You've got this! Environmental hygiene simply means managing our surroundings so that germs and hazards don't make people sick in the first place.

question: Why do we call environmental hygiene the foundation of preventive medicine?

options.A: It guarantees complete immunity against all viral infections
options.B: It replaces the need for surgical interventions in hospitals
options.C: It focuses solely on treating patients after they show symptoms
options.D: It stops illnesses before they start by controlling external hazards

explanation: Spot on! By cleaning up our surroundings early, we block diseases before they even get a chance to infect our patients.

question: What is the main purpose of having good sanitation facilities?

options.A: Safe disposal of human waste
options.B: Production of clean drinking water
options.C: Elimination of flying insect pests
options.D: Reduction of indoor air pollution

explanation: Great job! Sanitation is all about making sure human waste is handled safely so it doesn't contaminate our environment or spread disease.

question: How does handwashing with soap protect a community?

options.A: It kills all bacteria permanently so hands never get dirty again
options.B: It creates an impermeable barrier against toxic chemical spills
options.C: It replaces the need for cleaning hospital and clinic surfaces
options.D: It breaks the chain of infection by removing germs from skin

explanation: You nailed it! Simple handwashing physically washes away pathogens, stopping them from hitching a ride to food, surfaces, or other people.

question: What is the simplest way families can kill germs in drinking water at home?

options.A: Filtration
options.B: Boiling
options.C: Freezing
options.D: Sedimentation

explanation: That's right! Bringing water to a rolling boil is a quick, reliable way to kill disease-causing organisms right in your kitchen.

question: A family's well water is muddy with visible dirt particles. What should they do first before treating it?

options.A: Boil the muddy water without any preparation
options.B: Drink the water quickly before particles dissolve
options.C: Allow the water to undergo sedimentation
options.D: Add large amounts of liquid bleach immediately

explanation: Spot on! Letting the heavy dirt settle to the bottom first (sedimentation) makes cleaning or boiling the water much more effective.

question: What is the golden rule for managing different kinds of waste safely?

options.A: Dumping liquid waste near water wells
options.B: Segregation at the source
options.C: Burning everything in an open field
options.D: Mixing all refuse together to save time

explanation: You got it! Sorting waste right where you drop it keeps dangerous things like used needles away from regular household trash.

question: Why must medical waste be burned in an incinerator or buried deep instead of going to a normal dump?

options.A: It is required to generate electricity for local hospitals
options.B: It eliminates the need for any kind of protective clothing
options.C: It prevents injuries and the spread of infectious pathogens
options.D: It turns hazardous waste into edible organic fertilizer

explanation: Well done! Hospital waste carries germs and sharps that can easily harm waste workers and the community if not safely destroyed.

question: Which insect spreads the parasite that causes malaria?

options.A: Cockroach
options.B: Housefly
options.C: Mosquito
options.D: Termite

explanation: Correct! Female Anopheles mosquitoes carry and pass on the malaria parasite when they bite for a blood meal.

question: Why does clearing stagnant water around your compound help stop malaria?

options.A: It destroys the breeding sites where mosquitoes lay their eggs
options.B: It cools down the ambient temperature to kill flying insects
options.C: It prevents houseflies from walking on contaminated garbage
options.D: It poisons adult rats before they can enter the kitchen

explanation: Spot on! Mosquitoes need standing water to lay their eggs and grow. No stagnant water means fewer mosquitoes!

question: Which group of people suffers the most from poor environmental hygiene?

options.A: Teenagers in secondary schools
options.B: Children under five years old
options.C: Middle-aged office workers
options.D: Healthy young adult athletes

explanation: You're right! Little ones are still developing their immunity, making them extra vulnerable to severe dehydration from tummy bugs.

question: How does keeping a community clean actually help family finances?

options.A: Governments no longer need to collect any domestic taxes
options.B: Families spend less money on medications for preventable illnesses
options.C: Agricultural crop prices drop instantly in local markets
options.D: Hospitals can close down completely due to a lack of patients

explanation: Exactly! When people stay healthy, families save the money they would have spent treating repeated infections.

question: As a nurse, what is one of your main duties when it comes to environmental health?

options.A: Paving dirt roads to prevent dust inhalation in villages
options.B: Manufacturing chemical disinfectants in pharmaceutical labs
options.C: Educating patients and communities on hygiene practices
options.D: Constructing modern sewage treatment plants for cities

explanation: Spot on, future nurse! Teaching patients how to keep their homes and habits clean is a huge part of community health nursing.

question: A child keeps coming back to the clinic with severe diarrhea. What should you check first?

options.A: Assessing the family's source of drinking water and home sanitation
options.B: Telling the mother to stop feeding the child local home-cooked meals
options.C: Prescribing stronger antibiotics and keeping the child in the ward
options.D: Advising the parents to move to a different country entirely

explanation: Brilliant clinical thinking! Repeated diarrhea usually points to dirty water or poor home hygiene, so checking the root cause stops the cycle.

question: What is the primary purpose of a general physical examination?

options.A: To diagnose complex psychiatric disorders independently
options.B: To replace the need for laboratory diagnostic testing
options.C: To prescribe appropriate pharmacological interventions
options.D: To gather baseline data about a patient's health status

explanation: A general exam is primarily done to establish a baseline of physical health so nurses can track changes over time. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T1#GNS112_U6_T1_h1)

question: Why does a nurse perform a head-to-toe examination instead of only checking the patient's main complaint?

options.A: To detect subtle changes and physical signs of illness across all body systems
options.B: To fulfill hospital administrative requirements without clinical benefit
options.C: To quickly discharge the patient from the ward without delay
options.D: To avoid having to ask the patient about their medical history

explanation: Looking at the whole person helps uncover hidden issues that might be related to, or worsened by, the main complaint. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T1#GNS112_U6_T1_h1)

question: Why should a patient empty their bladder before a physical examination?

options.A: To collect a routine midstream urine sample automatically
options.B: To prevent the patient from falling asleep during the assessment
options.C: To reduce the overall weight of the patient before weighing
options.D: To ensure patient comfort during abdominal palpation

explanation: An empty bladder prevents discomfort and pressure when the nurse presses on the lower abdomen. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T1#GNS112_U6_T1_h2)

question: What is the main reason for explaining each step of the exam to the patient?

options.A: To fulfill a legal requirement for surgical consent
options.B: To reduce anxiety and build trust between nurse and patient
options.C: To train the patient to perform their own physical assessment
options.D: To speed up the total time spent at the bedside

explanation: Clear communication helps the patient relax, making the assessment easier and more accurate. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T1#GNS112_U6_T1_h2)

question: When should hand hygiene be performed during a physical examination?

options.A: At the end of the entire shift
options.B: Only when the patient has a known infection
options.C: Before and after touching the patient
options.D: Only if the nurse's hands look visibly dirty

explanation: Hand hygiene is the single most effective way to stop the spread of germs between patients and healthcare workers. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T1#GNS112_U6_T1_h3)

question: Why must reusable equipment like stethoscopes be wiped with disinfectant between patients?

options.A: To prevent cross-contamination and hospital-acquired infections
options.B: To keep the metal parts from rusting in humid weather
options.C: To remove any manufacturer dust from the surface
options.D: To ensure the sound quality remains clear for hearing

explanation: Medical tools can easily carry germs from one patient to another if they are not cleaned properly. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T1#GNS112_U6_T1_h3)

question: When does the general survey of a patient actually begin?

options.A: After listening to the patient's heart and lungs
options.B: When the blood pressure cuff is inflated
options.C: When writing the final discharge notes
options.D: The moment the nurse first sees the patient

explanation: The general survey starts immediately through observation before any hands-on examination takes place. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T1#GNS112_U6_T1_h4)

question: A nurse walks into a room and notices a patient clutching their chest and breathing heavily. What category of the general survey does this fall under?

options.A: Personal hygiene
options.B: Level of consciousness
options.C: Nutritional status
options.D: Signs of distress

explanation: Clutching the chest and heavy breathing are immediate physical indicators of acute distress. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T1#GNS112_U6_T1_h4)

question: Which measurement is frequently referred to as the fifth vital sign?

options.A: Weight
options.B: Height
options.C: Urinary output
options.D: Pain

explanation: Pain is routinely assessed alongside traditional vital signs to monitor patient comfort and well-being. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T1#GNS112_U6_T1_h5)

question: Why is it important to use the correct blood pressure cuff size?

options.A: It prevents the patient from feeling any pressure at all
options.B: An incorrect size leads to inaccurate blood pressure readings
options.C: Hospital regulations require matching cuffs to patient age only
options.D: Small cuffs are easier to wrap around the arm quickly

explanation: A cuff that is too small gives a falsely high reading, while one that is too large gives a falsely low reading. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T1#GNS112_U6_T1_h5)

question: What is the correct order of assessment techniques for most body parts?

options.A: Percussion, auscultation, palpation, inspection
options.B: Palpation, inspection, auscultation, percussion
options.C: Inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation
options.D: Auscultation, percussion, inspection, palpation

explanation: For most body systems, you look first, feel second, tap third, and listen last. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T1#GNS112_U6_T1_h6)

question: Why is the sequence of techniques changed when examining the abdomen?

options.A: Auscultation is done first so pressing on the belly does not change bowel sounds
options.B: Percussion is omitted entirely to prevent patient discomfort
options.C: Inspection is skipped because visual data is unreliable
options.D: Palpation must be done first to locate hidden organs before listening

explanation: Touching or pressing the abdomen can stimulate bowel activity, giving a false impression of bowel sounds. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T1#GNS112_U6_T1_h6)

question: What type of language should a nurse use when documenting physical exam findings?

options.A: Vague and generalized terms like 'fine'
options.B: Subjective opinions about the patient's attitude
options.C: Clear, objective, and descriptive language
options.D: Complex poetic metaphors to describe wounds

explanation: Objective descriptions prevent confusion and provide clear facts for other healthcare providers. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T1#GNS112_U6_T1_h7)

question: Why is timely documentation of assessment findings important for patient care?

options.A: It is only required for billing and insurance purposes
options.B: It prevents patients from reading their own medical charts
options.C: It ensures continuity of care and accurate communication across shifts
options.D: It allows the nurse to leave the hospital premises much earlier

explanation: Prompt charting lets the next nurse or doctor know the exact status of the patient without relying on memory. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T1#GNS112_U6_T1_h7)

question: What are the standard cardinal signs evaluated during a routine physical assessment?

options.A: Temperature, pulse, respiration, and blood pressure
options.B: Pain level, reflex response, pupil size, and skin color
options.C: Mental status, urine output, bowel sounds, and core temperature
options.D: Weight, height, blood glucose, and visual acuity

explanation: The four classic cardinal vital signs reflect the most critical life-sustaining physiological functions of the body. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h1)

question: Why do nurses take a baseline set of vital signs when a patient is first admitted?

options.A: It gives a standard reference point to detect future clinical changes
options.B: It prevents the patient from developing hospital-acquired infections
options.C: It determines the exact medical diagnosis without needing lab tests
options.D: It fulfills the legal requirement to discharge the patient safely

explanation: Having an accurate starting measurement helps you immediately spot when your patient's condition starts getting worse. Great job thinking like a nurse! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h1)

question: Which temperature route gives the closest measurement of the body's core temperature?

options.A: Tympanic
options.B: Rectal
options.C: Axillary
options.D: Oral

explanation: Because it's taken inside the body cavity, a rectal reading is the most accurate reflection of true core temperature. You've got this! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h2)

question: What is the medical term for an elevated body temperature caused by an infection?

options.A: Hypothermia
options.B: Bradycardia
options.C: Pyrexia
options.D: Hypotension

explanation: Pyrexia is just the clinical word for a fever! It happens when the body intentionally raises its set point to fight off germs. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h2)

question: What is the normal resting pulse rate for a healthy adult?

options.A: 60 to 100 beats per minute
options.B: 40 to 60 beats per minute
options.C: 100 to 140 beats per minute
options.D: 80 to 120 beats per minute

explanation: A normal adult heart rate at rest falls safely between 60 and 100 beats per minute. Keep this number handy for your ward practice! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h3)

question: Why should you avoid using your thumb when checking a patient's radial pulse?

options.A: Using the thumb violates standard hospital infection control rules
options.B: The thumb has its own distinct pulse that can confuse the count
options.C: The thumb applies too much pressure and collapses the artery
options.D: The thumb is too insensitive to feel the soft arterial wall

explanation: Your thumb has its own strong pulse! If you use it, you might end up counting your own heartbeat instead of the patient's. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h3)

question: What is the normal resting breathing rate for a healthy adult?

options.A: 30 to 40 breaths per minute
options.B: 8 to 12 breaths per minute
options.C: 20 to 30 breaths per minute
options.D: 12 to 20 breaths per minute

explanation: Healthy adults take between 12 and 20 breaths every minute while resting. Easy to remember for your exams! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h4)

question: Why is it best to count a patient's breathing rate discreetly without telling them right away?

options.A: It saves time during a busy hospital shift to count during pulse checks
options.B: Patients will feel anxious if they know their lungs are being watched
options.C: Unconscious patients are the only ones who have true resting rates
options.D: Conscious awareness can alter the patient's normal breathing rate and depth

explanation: When people know you are watching them breathe, they naturally start controlling it. Counting while pretending to check the pulse is a smart clinical trick! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h4)

question: What does the top number in a blood pressure reading represent?

options.A: Systolic pressure during heart contraction
options.B: Diastolic pressure during heart relaxation
options.C: Mean arterial pressure across the cardiac cycle
options.D: Central venous pressure inside the right atrium

explanation: The systolic (top) number measures the peak pressure in your arteries when the heart pumps. You're mastering the basics! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h5)

question: What happens to a blood pressure reading if you use a cuff that is way too narrow for the patient's arm?

options.A: The reading will be falsely high
options.B: The blood pressure cannot be measured at all
options.C: The reading will be falsely low
options.D: The reading will remain completely normal

explanation: A narrow cuff needs extra squeeze to block the artery in a bigger arm, which tricks the machine or gauge into showing a falsely high reading. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h5)

question: What heart action directly causes the apex beat you feel on the chest?

options.A: Filling of the right atrium during diastole
options.B: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves
options.C: Contraction of the left ventricle during systole
options.D: Opening of the tricuspid and mitral valves

explanation: When the left ventricle squeezes, it twists forward and taps against the chest wall, creating that palpable apex beat. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h6)

question: Which part of the heart forms the tip that hits the chest wall during a heartbeat?

options.A: The lower tip of the left ventricle
options.B: The middle wall dividing the ventricles
options.C: The upper base of the right atrium
options.D: The outer surface of the right atrium

explanation: The bottom tip (inferior tip) of the left ventricle makes up the apex of the heart that touches your stethoscope or fingers. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h6)

question: Where is the normal point of maximal impulse (PMI) located on a healthy adult chest?

options.A: Second intercostal space at the left sternal border
options.B: Third intercostal space at the right sternal border
options.C: Seventh intercostal space at the anterior axillary line
options.D: Fifth intercostal space at the left midclavicular line

explanation: You'll usually find the normal PMI right at the fifth intercostal space along the left midclavicular line. Excellent clinical landmark! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h7)

question: If you find a patient's PMI shifted far to the left, what does that usually suggest?

options.A: Collapse of the right lung
options.B: Normal athletic heart conditioning
options.C: Dehydration and low blood volume
options.D: Enlargement of the heart

explanation: When the heart muscle gets bigger or stretched out, the PMI moves downward and outward to the left. Spotting this helps you catch complications early! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h7)

question: What is the term for a resting heart rate that drops below 60 beats per minute?

options.A: Tachypnea
options.B: Bradycardia
options.C: Hypotension
options.D: Tachycardia

explanation: Bradycardia simply means a slow heart rate (under 60 bpm in adults). You are building a strong clinical vocabulary! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h8)

question: Which of these findings is completely normal and NOT a sign of heart stress?

options.A: A resting heart rate of 120 beats per minute
options.B: A regular resting pulse rate of 75 beats per minute
options.C: A blood pressure reading consistently above 140/90 mmHg
options.D: An apex beat displaced far to the left of the midclavicular line

explanation: A pulse of 75 bpm sits right in the middle of the normal 60–100 range. Nothing to worry about here! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h8)

question: When is the best time to record a patient's vital signs in their chart?

options.A: At the very end of the working shift
options.B: Whenever the physician asks for past notes
options.C: Only if the patient shows abnormal symptoms
options.D: Promptly after completing the assessment

explanation: Always document right away! Doing it immediately prevents mix-ups and keeps patient care safe and reliable. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h9)

question: Why is it crucial to quickly report abnormal vital signs to the doctor?

options.A: It ensures the hospital bed can be reassigned to another patient quickly
options.B: It proves the nurse completed all assigned tasks for the morning
options.C: It allows the healthcare team to intervene before the patient's condition worsens
options.D: It removes the need to monitor the patient for the rest of the day

explanation: Quick communication lets the medical team step in fast and prevent emergencies. Your quick thinking saves lives! [learn more](GNS112_U6_T2#GNS112_U6_T2_h9)

question: What is the main clinical purpose of performing basic anthropometric measurements in a hospital?

options.A: To measure the electrical activity of the heart
options.B: To evaluate nutritional status and help calculate drug doses
options.C: To diagnose specific infectious diseases quickly
options.D: To check how well the lungs exchange oxygen

explanation: Height and weight provide essential baseline numbers used directly to assess general health and safely figure out proper medication dosages. [learn more](GNS112_U6_T3#GNS112_U6_T3_h1)

question: Why should a nurse always measure height and weight accurately instead of just guessing?

options.A: Inaccurate numbers can lead to dangerous errors in medication dosing
options.B: Patients get offended if the nurse guesses their size
options.C: Estimated numbers make the patient chart look untidy
options.D: Hospital management requires exact figures for billing purposes only

explanation: Many strong drugs, especially for children and critically ill patients, depend on exact body measurements so you don't accidentally give too much or too little. Great job learning the safety rules!

question: What is the first thing a nurse should do with a mechanical weighing scale before a patient steps on it?

options.A: Wipe the platform with hot cooking oil
options.B: Place a thick mat underneath it
options.C: Lock the height rod permanently
options.D: Calibrate and balance it to zero

explanation: Always check that the scale starts right at zero! This ensures your weight reading is accurate and not thrown off by a previous reading.

question: A patient steps onto the clinic scale wearing heavy leather boots and a thick jacket. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Subtract two kilograms manually in your head and record that number
options.B: Proceed with the measurement as is since clothing weight does not matter
options.C: Ask the patient to remove the boots and heavy jacket before weighing
options.D: Refuse to measure the patient until another day

explanation: Heavy shoes and clothes add extra weight to the scale. Asking the patient to take them off gives you a true and accurate reading!

question: Which tool is best for measuring the standing height of an adult patient?

options.A: Knee height calipers
options.B: An infant length board
options.C: A stadiometer
options.D: A flexible cloth sewing tape

explanation: A stadiometer is the standard tool with a vertical backboard and sliding headpiece built specifically to measure standing height accurately.

question: Why do you usually need two healthcare workers to measure the length of a baby?

options.A: One person writes down the numbers while the other watches the monitor
options.B: One holds the head steady while the other straightens the legs and moves the footboard
options.C: Infants are too heavy for a single nurse to lift onto the measuring table
options.D: Hospital policy strictly forbids any nurse from working alone with babies

explanation: Babies wiggle a lot! Having one person hold the head safely while the second person gently straightens the legs gets you an accurate measurement.

question: What time of day is best for taking a patient's daily weight to get a reliable comparison?

options.A: Immediately after a large dinner
options.B: Late in the evening before sleep
options.C: In the morning after voiding
options.D: Right after finishing afternoon tea

explanation: Weighing in the morning after the bladder is emptied helps avoid the changes in weight caused by food and fluids taken throughout the day.

question: A bedridden patient on fluid restriction needs a daily weight check. What is the most important step to make sure the reading is correct?

options.A: Remove all intravenous lines temporarily during the weighing process
options.B: Use a standard bathroom floor scale slid underneath the mattress
options.C: Weigh the patient only when visitors are present to help
options.D: Ensure the bedding and drainage tubes are arranged consistently or zeroed out

explanation: Extra blankets, pillows, or full drainage bags left on a bed scale will add false weight. Always keep bed setups consistent or zero them out!

question: What does a high waist circumference mostly tell you about a patient's health risk?

options.A: Severe protein deficiency and muscle wasting
options.B: A normal and healthy distribution of total body water
options.C: Excess visceral fat linked to heart disease and diabetes
options.D: Chronic lung disease and poor oxygen exchange

explanation: Fat stored around the belly and internal organs is strongly linked to a higher risk of heart problems and diabetes. Excellent clinical insight!

question: Why is Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) so popular during community outreaches and emergencies?

options.A: It replaces the need to ever measure a patient's height or weight
options.B: It is quick, requires minimal inexpensive equipment, and effectively screens for malnutrition
options.C: It is the only accurate way to calculate an adult surgical patient's drug dosage
options.D: It provides a direct measurement of blood pressure and pulse rate

explanation: MUAC tapes are cheap, portable, and fast, making them perfect for checking nutrition quickly when you don't have a scale handy.

question: Which two measurements do you need to calculate a patient's Body Mass Index (BMI)?

options.A: Weight and height
options.B: Waist size and age
options.C: Arm span and chest girth
options.D: Blood pressure and weight

explanation: BMI is calculated simply by taking the patient's weight and dividing it by their height squared.

question: What is a major limitation of relying only on BMI to judge someone's health?

options.A: It changes drastically depending on what the patient ate for breakfast
options.B: It requires expensive laboratory equipment to calculate properly
options.C: It only works accurately for newborn infants and toddlers
options.D: It cannot distinguish between weight coming from muscle mass versus body fat

explanation: Muscle weighs more than fat, meaning a very muscular athlete might show up as overweight on a BMI chart even when they are super healthy!

question: Why do nurses routinely measure head circumference in infants and toddlers during clinic visits?

options.A: To screen for potential neurological or brain development issues
options.B: To check if the child has a normal chest expansion rate
options.C: To calculate the exact caloric intake needed for daily growth
options.D: To determine what shoe size the child will wear as an adult

explanation: Head growth goes hand-in-hand with brain development. Tracking it helps catch issues like fluid buildup in the brain early on.

question: What is the best way to interpret a child's weight measurement in a clinic?

options.A: Averaging the weight reading with the mother's weight
options.B: Plotting the measurement on a growth chart to observe the growth trend over time
options.C: Checking if the weight matches the child's shoe size and hair color
options.D: Comparing the child's weight directly to the average weight of an adult

explanation: A single number doesn't tell the whole story. Seeing how the weight tracks on a growth curve over months shows the true picture of health!

question: Which units are standard for recording height and weight in clinical nursing notes?

options.A: Feet and pounds
options.B: Centimeters and kilograms
options.C: Millimeters and grams
options.D: Inches and stones

explanation: Hospitals use the metric system (centimeters and kilograms) worldwide to keep records clear and prevent medication dosing mistakes.

question: A nurse needs to weigh a patient wearing a heavy leg cast that cannot be taken off. How should this be documented?

options.A: Guess how much the cast weighs and subtract that amount from the scale reading
options.B: Record the weight and add a clear note stating the patient was wearing a leg cast
options.C: Omit the weight entry entirely from the patient chart until the cast comes off
options.D: Record the weight without any mention of the cast so the chart looks normal

explanation: Always document the facts! Adding a note about the cast helps other nurses understand why the weight is higher without guessing.

question: What exactly is a 'specimen' when you are caring for a patient?

options.A: A sterile instrument used during a surgical procedure
options.B: A prescribed medication dose given during a shift
options.C: A sample of tissue or body fluid taken for laboratory examination
options.D: A written record of the patient daily vital signs

explanation: A specimen is simply any biological sample (like blood or urine) collected from a patient to help run lab tests. You'll be collecting these all the time!

question: Why must you, as the nurse, use great care when collecting laboratory specimens?

options.A: It decreases the overall cost of running hospital diagnostic equipment
options.B: It ensures the lab results reflect the true condition of the patient
options.C: It shortens the length of time the patient stays in the hospital
options.D: It removes the need for doctors to physically examine the patient

explanation: Spot-on! Good collection habits prevent errors and contamination, meaning the doctor gets accurate results to treat your patient properly.

question: What is the single best way to stop germs from spreading when handling specimens?

options.A: Changing the patient room air filters daily
options.B: Wearing two pairs of sterile gloves at all times
options.C: Spraying the examination table with bleach
options.D: Proper hand hygiene before and after the procedure

explanation: Simple handwashing remains your greatest superpower in infection control. Wash your hands religiously!

question: What should you do immediately after using a needle to draw blood?

options.A: Carefully scoop the needle cap back on using one hand to prevent injury
options.B: Place the needle on a clean tray until the end of the shift
options.C: Break the needle tip off with forceps before throwing it in the bin
options.D: Drop the unrecapped needle directly into a puncture-resistant sharps container

explanation: Never recap needles! Dropping them straight into the sharps box right beside you is the safest way to avoid accidental needle-pricks.

question: Why do we prefer a 'clean-catch midstream' urine sample when checking for a urinary tract infection?

options.A: It contains a higher concentration of red blood cells
options.B: It requires less total volume than a random urine sample
options.C: It eliminates the need for any patient preparation
options.D: It avoids collecting bacteria from around the urethral opening

explanation: By letting the first bit of urine flush away skin germs, the midstream sample gives a true picture of what is actually inside the urinary tract.

question: How do you properly start a 24-hour urine collection test for a patient?

options.A: Save all urine produced starting from midnight regardless of when the patient last urinated
options.B: Collect the very first morning urine sample and use that exact time to start the 24-hour clock
options.C: Wait until the patient drinks two liters of water before collecting the first sample
options.D: Have the patient empty their bladder completely, discard that urine, and start the timer

explanation: Always throw away that very first void to empty the bladder completely, then start your 24-hour clock with a clean slate!

question: Which everyday substance must definitely be kept out of a stool sample?

options.A: Normal saline
options.B: Tap water
options.C: Paper towels
options.D: Urine

explanation: Urine mixes easily with stool and can ruin lab tests for parasites or blood. Always ask patients to pass urine first!

question: What does a black, tarry stool sample usually tell you about your patient?

options.A: Bleeding in the upper gastrointestinal tract
options.B: Bleeding in the lower rectum or anus
options.C: Severe dehydration and low fluid intake
options.D: A high intake of green leafy vegetables

explanation: As blood travels all the way from the stomach through the gut, digestive juices break it down, turning it dark and tarry by the time it comes out.

question: When is the best time of day to collect a sputum (phlegm) sample?

options.A: Just before the patient goes to sleep at night
options.B: Right after the patient takes a warm shower
options.C: Immediately after a heavy lunch or dinner meal
options.D: Early in the morning before eating or drinking

explanation: Secretions pool in the airways overnight, making early morning the absolute best time to catch a good deep cough sample.

question: How is true sputum different from ordinary saliva?

options.A: Saliva is thick and colored green or yellow due to infection
options.B: Sputum is produced entirely by glands inside the oral cavity
options.C: Saliva contains high amounts of blood and cellular debris
options.D: Sputum comes from deep in the lungs and lower respiratory tract

explanation: Saliva is just mouth fluid, but sputum comes coughing up from the lungs and bronchial tubes, which is what the lab needs to see.

question: If a patient vomits something that looks like coffee grounds, what does that usually mean?

options.A: Partially digested blood from the stomach
options.B: A complete blockage of the large intestine
options.C: The recent consumption of dark roasted coffee
options.D: Excessive production of normal bile fluid

explanation: Classic clinical sign! Stomach acid reacts with bleeding in the upper GI tract, giving old blood that distinct coffee-ground texture.

question: Why might a patient's vomit turn a bright green or yellow color?

options.A: It is a normal sign of eating green vegetables
options.B: It indicates that food was digested properly in the small intestine
options.C: It proves the patient has a severe bacterial lung infection
options.D: It often appears after prolonged vomiting when the stomach is empty

explanation: Once the stomach is completely empty from throwing up, continuous vomiting brings up bright green or yellow bile from the small intestine.

question: At what point should you label a specimen container with the patient details?

options.A: Only after the laboratory technician asks for confirmation
options.B: Immediately at the bedside in the presence of the patient
options.C: After returning to the nursing station at the end of the shift
options.D: Before entering the patient room to save working time

explanation: Always label right at the bedside! Doing it later invites dangerous mix-ups between patients.

question: What is the main danger of leaving a collected lab specimen sitting at room temperature for too long?

options.A: Bacteria can multiply and cells can break down, giving false results
options.B: The label on the container will automatically fade and fall off
options.C: The specimen container will become legally invalid for testing
options.D: Hospital management will issue a fine for delayed paperwork

explanation: Time matters! Leaving samples sitting around lets bacteria multiply or cells decay, which ruins the accuracy of the test.

question: What two main changes happen in the blood during asphyxia?

options.A: High sodium and low potassium
options.B: Low oxygen and high carbon dioxide
options.C: High oxygen and low carbon dioxide
options.D: Low glucose and high lactic acid

explanation: Think of asphyxia as a double hit: oxygen isn't getting in, and carbon dioxide gets trapped because the lungs aren't exchanging gases properly. You've got this!

question: Why does the body quickly develop metabolic acidosis during severe asphyxia?

options.A: Anaerobic metabolism produces excess lactic acid
options.B: Liver cells release stored hydrochloric acid
options.C: Lungs absorb too much environmental nitrogen
options.D: The kidneys stop filtering urea completely

explanation: When cells are starved of oxygen, they switch to emergency backup power (anaerobic metabolism). This backup mode makes energy, but it leaves behind a lot of lactic acid, which makes the blood acidic. Great job reviewing your metabolism basics!

question: Which of these is a classic example of environmental asphyxia?

options.A: Severe diabetic ketoacidosis
options.B: An acute myocardial infarction
options.C: Drowning in a swimming pool
options.D: A sudden allergic asthma attack

explanation: Environmental asphyxia happens when outside factors—like water, smoke, or a tight space—keep a person from reaching clean air. Water in a pool is a clear external block!

question: How does carbon monoxide poisoning cause internal suffocation?

options.A: It directly paralyzes the diaphragm muscle
options.B: It triggers immediate swelling of the vocal cords
options.C: It causes the lungs to fill with fluid rapidly
options.D: It binds to hemoglobin and blocks oxygen delivery

explanation: Carbon monoxide is sneaky—it loves sticking to your red blood cells (hemoglobin) way more than oxygen does. Even if the patient is breathing fine, their tissues still starve because the seats on the transport truck are all taken!

question: What physical sign usually shows up during the second stage of progressive asphyxia?

options.A: Complete paralysis of all four limbs
options.B: Cyanosis and muscle convulsions
options.C: Flushed skin and sudden hyperactivity
options.D: Uncontrolled high fever and sweating

explanation: As the body runs lower on oxygen, the skin turns a bluish color (cyanosis), and the oxygen-starved brain starts misfiring, leading to muscle twitching or seizures.

question: What does a patient's breathing pattern usually look like right before respiratory arrest?

options.A: It stops instantly without any warning signs
options.B: It becomes perfectly regular and extremely deep
options.C: It changes into slow, gasping, and irregular breaths
options.D: It speeds up to over sixty breaths per minute

explanation: Right before breathing gives out completely, the brain's breathing center struggles hard, resulting in slow, strange gasps known as agonal breathing.

question: Which heart sign usually appears late in severe, untreated asphyxia?

options.A: Bounding hypertension
options.B: Severe bradycardia
options.C: Rapid atrial flutter
options.D: Normal sinus rhythm

explanation: At first, the heart pumps faster to cope with the stress. But as the lack of oxygen drags on, the heart muscle gets tired and weak, causing the heart rate to drop dangerously low (bradycardia).

question: A patient pulled from a smoky room is restless, confused, and breathing fast. What do these signs tell you first?

options.A: Primary psychiatric panic disorder
options.B: Inadequate oxygen delivery to the brain
options.C: A normal reaction to a stressful environment
options.D: Severe dehydration and electrolyte imbalance

explanation: The brain is very sensitive! Confusion and restlessness are classic early distress signals letting you know the brain isn't getting enough oxygen to think clearly.

question: What is your absolute first priority when managing a patient with acute asphyxia?

options.A: Obtaining a detailed medical history from family
options.B: Drawing arterial blood gas samples for testing
options.C: Inserting an intravenous line for medications
options.D: Ensuring a patent airway and providing oxygen

explanation: Airway and breathing always come first (think ABCs!). The brain starts dying within minutes without oxygen, so restoring airflow beats paperwork or IV lines every time.

question: You are bagging an unresponsive patient with a bag-valve-mask, but their chest isn't rising. What should you do next?

options.A: Disconnect the oxygen tubing from the wall supply
options.B: Turn the patient onto their side in the recovery position
options.C: Squeeze the ventilation bag much harder and faster
options.D: Reposition the head and check the airway for blockage

explanation: If air isn't going in, don't just squeeze harder! Check for a blockage and readjust the head position to open up that airway properly. You're doing great.

question: Which test is most helpful for checking acid-base balance after an asphyxial event?

options.A: Arterial blood gas analysis
options.B: Routine urinalysis dipstick
options.C: Serum electrolyte panel
options.D: Complete blood cell count

explanation: An ABG test is your best friend here. It gives you a direct look at the patient's blood pH, oxygen levels, and how well they are clearing out carbon dioxide.

question: Why is keeping a close eye on a recovering patient's nervous system so important after asphyxia?

options.A: To prevent the development of peripheral edema
options.B: To detect early signs of secondary brain injury
options.C: To calculate the correct maintenance fluid rate
options.D: To measure the exact volume of daily urine output

explanation: Brain tissue hates being starved of oxygen. Even after breathing is restored, nurses monitor neuro status closely to catch any delayed swelling or drops in consciousness right away.

question: What does the term 'hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy' mean?

options.A: Sudden inflammation of the peripheral nerve endings
options.B: An infection of the lining surrounding the spinal cord
options.C: Brain injury caused by oxygen and blood deprivation
options.D: A chronic degenerative disease of the liver tissue

explanation: Let's break down the big words: 'hypoxic' (low oxygen), 'ischemic' (low blood flow), and 'encephalopathy' (brain trouble). Put it together, and it's brain injury from lack of oxygen and blood!

question: Why do the kidneys often take a hit during prolonged body-wide asphyxia?

options.A: Lactic acid crystals block the small ureter tubes
options.B: They absorb too much carbon dioxide from the blood
options.C: They experience severe reduction in blood perfusion
options.D: The kidneys overproduce urine to flush out toxins

explanation: When the body runs low on oxygen, it goes into survival mode, pulling blood away from the kidneys and skin to protect the brain and heart. Sadly, this leaves the kidneys starved and vulnerable to damage.

question: When moving an injured person, what is the most important goal to keep in mind?

options.A: Reaching the nearest hospital in the shortest possible time
options.B: Ensuring the patient's family members can ride along
options.C: Clearing the emergency scene before law enforcement arrives
options.D: Moving the patient safely without causing further injury

explanation: You've got this! Safety and protecting the patient from extra harm always come first, even before rushing to the hospital. Great nursing instincts!

question: Why shouldn't you rush or speed too much when transporting an accident victim?

options.A: Vehicles consume too much fuel when driven too fast
options.B: Rushing can compromise the airway or worsen existing injuries
options.C: Hospitals prefer patients to arrive slowly for administrative reasons
options.D: Rescuers get too tired to document the incident properly

explanation: Spot on! Moving too fast without control can cause dropped stretchers or mess up breathing tubes. Smooth and steady wins the race in emergency care.

question: In the emergency ABCDE assessment check, what does the letter 'B' stand for?

options.A: Breathing
options.B: Blood pressure
options.C: Bone
options.D: Bleeding

explanation: Easy and correct! 'B' stands for Breathing. Checking chest movement is one of the very first things we do for any emergency patient.

question: You are getting a trauma patient ready for an ambulance ride. What must you check and do FIRST?

options.A: Notifying the receiving physician of the patient's insurance status
options.B: Completing the detailed nursing admission notes
options.C: Washing and dressing all minor abrasions
options.D: Securing an open airway and controlling severe bleeding

explanation: Well done! Life-saving care always comes before paperwork or minor cuts. ABC comes first!

question: What is the best position for transporting an unconscious patient who is still breathing and has a pulse?

options.A: High Fowler's position
options.B: Prone position
options.C: Recovery position
options.D: Trendelenburg position

explanation: Brilliant! Placing them on their side (recovery position) keeps the tongue from blocking the airway and lets any fluids drain safely.

question: Why do we keep a patient with a suspected spinal injury flat on a hard board?

options.A: To make it easier to slide them into the back of an ambulance
options.B: To reduce the overall weight of the patient during lifting
options.C: To allow the nurse to check the abdomen more frequently
options.D: To prevent twisting or bending of the spinal column

explanation: Exactly right! A rigid board stops any accidental bending that could cause permanent damage to the spinal cord.

question: Which type of stretcher splits into two halves so you can slide it under a patient without rolling them?

options.A: Scoop stretcher
options.B: Basket stretcher
options.C: Canvas folding stretcher
options.D: Rigid spine board

explanation: Spot on! A scoop stretcher splits lengthwise, making it super helpful when you want to avoid rolling a fragile patient.

question: When is a basket stretcher (Stokes litter) most useful during a rescue?

options.A: For moving stable patients down smooth hospital hallways
options.B: During rough terrain, outdoor rescue operations, or hoisting
options.C: For quick transfers from a bed to a bathroom shower chair
options.D: When a patient requires immediate open-heart surgery in transit

explanation: You got it! The cage-like design protects the patient securely when navigating rough paths, stairs, or rocky areas.

question: What is the safest way to bend your body when lifting a heavy patient or equipment?

options.A: By leaning to one side
options.B: At the waist only
options.C: At the hips and knees
options.D: With legs completely straight

explanation: Awesome! Always lift with your legs (knees and hips bent), not your back, to protect your spine from injury.

question: Why should you avoid twisting your body while carrying a heavy load?

options.A: It causes the rescue team to lose their sense of direction
options.B: It increases the air pressure inside the transport vehicle
options.C: It automatically makes the patient slide off the stretcher
options.D: It places excessive rotational stress on the lumbar spine disks

explanation: That's correct! Twisting while carrying something heavy is one of the fastest ways nurses hurt their lower backs. Protect your spine!

question: Why is keeping a close eye on your patient so crucial while moving them in an ambulance?

options.A: Transport equipment automatically records electrical brain waves
options.B: Vehicle motion and vibrations can mask or worsen clinical changes
options.C: Hospital regulations require a full report every sixty seconds
options.D: Patients sleep better when nurses talk to them constantly

explanation: Spot on! The bumps and vibrations of a moving vehicle can hide early signs of trouble, so constant monitoring is a must.

question: While in the ambulance, you notice the intravenous (IV) line has stopped flowing. What is the very first thing you should check?

options.A: Whether the tubing is kinked or the patient's arm is bent
options.B: Whether the patient's blood type needs to be re-checked
options.C: Whether the ambulance driver is speeding too fast
options.D: Whether the hospital pharmacy has more fluid in stock

explanation: Great clinical thinking! Movement in transit often causes IV tubing to bend or kink. Always check the line physically first.

question: What do the letters in the SBAR handover tool stand for?

options.A: System, Bedside, Analysis, Report
options.B: Symptoms, Breathing, Airway, Respiration
options.C: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation
options.D: Safety, Balance, Assessment, Recovery

explanation: You nailed it! SBAR is your best friend for giving quick, structured, and clear patient updates to other healthcare workers.

question: Why is a proper verbal and written handover necessary when bringing a patient to a new ward?

options.A: To prevent family members from asking questions about the bill
options.B: To satisfy insurance companies that the trip took place
options.C: To give the transport nurse an excuse to leave the hospital early
options.D: To ensure continuity of safe care and prevent important details from being lost

explanation: Exactly! A solid handover bridges the gap between transport and the new ward, keeping patient safety front and center.

question: What colour and flow pattern does arterial bleeding typically show?

options.A: Bright red and trickling evenly
options.B: Bright red and spurting in jets
options.C: Dark red and oozing slowly
options.D: Dark red and flowing in a steady stream

explanation: Arteries carry oxygenated blood under high pressure from the heart, causing it to spurt out in pulses when a vessel is cut. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T2#GNS112_U7_T2_h1)

question: Why is internal haemorrhage often harder to detect quickly than external haemorrhage?

options.A: Internal blood vessels do not contain red blood cells
options.B: The blood is hidden inside body cavities and tissues
options.C: Internal bleeding stops automatically without any medical help
options.D: The body instantly absorbs all escaped internal blood

explanation: Because the bleeding occurs within closed body spaces like the abdomen or chest, there is no visible sign on the skin surface. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T2#GNS112_U7_T2_h1)

question: What is the primary trigger for hypovolemic shock?

options.A: An infection spreading through the bloodstream
options.B: A rapid drop in circulating blood volume
options.C: An acute blockage in the coronary arteries
options.D: A sudden spike in blood pressure

explanation: Hypovolemic shock happens when the body loses a massive amount of fluid or blood, leaving the circulatory system with too little volume to fill the blood vessels. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T2#GNS112_U7_T2_h2)

question: Which organs are prioritized and receive redirected blood flow during early shock?

options.A: The kidneys and the stomach
options.B: The skin and the skeletal muscles
options.C: The liver and the intestines
options.D: The brain and the heart

explanation: The body's survival reflex constricts vessels in less vital areas like the skin and gut to ensure the brain and heart continue to receive oxygen. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T2#GNS112_U7_T2_h2)

question: Which of the following is an early physical sign of significant blood loss?

options.A: A fast heart rate
options.B: Flushed, warm skin
options.C: A very slow pulse
options.D: High urine output

explanation: The heart beats faster to pump the remaining blood volume harder and maintain cardiac output when blood is lost. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T2#GNS112_U7_T2_h3)

question: A young adult patient has lost a large amount of blood from a trauma, yet their blood pressure remains normal. What is the best explanation for this?

options.A: Young adults are immune to the effects of hypovolemic shock
options.B: The bleeding has completely stopped on its own
options.C: Strong blood vessel constriction is temporarily hiding the blood loss
options.D: The blood loss is minor and requires no further observation

explanation: Strong compensatory mechanisms in younger patients can keep blood pressure normal even after losing a dangerous amount of blood. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T2#GNS112_U7_T2_h3)

question: Why is measuring hourly urine output so important when monitoring a bleeding patient?

options.A: It is a reliable indicator of whether vital organs are receiving enough blood
options.B: It prevents the urinary bladder from becoming overstretched
options.C: It tells the nurse the exact blood type of the patient
options.D: It proves that the patient is drinking enough water by mouth

explanation: The kidneys are sensitive to drops in blood volume; if urine output falls, it means perfusion to major organs is inadequate. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T2#GNS112_U7_T2_h4)

question: When monitoring vital signs in a patient with suspected internal bleeding, what is most important to look for?

options.A: A single normal blood pressure reading
options.B: A sudden drop in body temperature
options.C: An increase in respiratory depth only
options.D: Trends indicating a worsening condition over time

explanation: Observing how vital signs change sequentially gives a much clearer picture of ongoing blood loss than looking at one isolated set of numbers. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T2#GNS112_U7_T2_h4)

question: What is the first and most effective step to control severe external bleeding from a limb wound?

options.A: Elevating the injured arm or leg above the heart
options.B: Giving the patient oral fluids immediately
options.C: Applying direct firm pressure to the wound
options.D: Washing the wound thoroughly with cold water

explanation: Direct pressure helps compress the damaged blood vessels and allows a blood clot to form over the injury site. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T2#GNS112_U7_T2_h5)

question: Why is keeping a severely bleeding patient warm an important part of first aid?

options.A: Warmth increases the amount of oxygen in red blood cells
options.B: Hypothermia causes the heart rate to slow down too much
options.C: Cold temperatures impair the body's natural blood clotting mechanisms
options.D: Patients in shock always feel feverish and uncomfortable

explanation: Hypothermia prevents the clotting cascade from working properly, making it much harder for the body to stop bleeding naturally. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T2#GNS112_U7_T2_h5)

question: What is the main purpose of giving a blood transfusion to a patient with acute haemorrhage?

options.A: To prevent the kidneys from producing any urine
options.B: To speed up the digestion of food in the stomach
options.C: To replace lost red blood cells and restore oxygen delivery
options.D: To lower the patient's elevated body temperature

explanation: Transfusions supply the red blood cells needed to carry oxygen to tissues when the patient's own blood volume is dangerously depleted. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T2#GNS112_U7_T2_h6)

question: Which intervention involves threading a catheter through blood vessels to block the bleeding site with tiny coils?

options.A: Interventional radiology embolization
options.B: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy
options.C: Endoscopic vessel clipping
options.D: Routine surgical wound suturing

explanation: Radiologists use imaging guidance to navigate inside blood vessels and place coils that block flow to bleeding arteries without major open surgery. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T2#GNS112_U7_T2_h6)

question: Which complication frequently develops following prolonged low blood pressure and shock from severe bleeding?

options.A: Acute kidney injury
options.B: Enlargement of the spleen
options.C: Excessive bone mineralization
options.D: Chronic high blood pressure

explanation: When blood flow drops significantly during shock, the kidneys suffer from oxygen deprivation, which can lead to acute kidney damage. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T2#GNS112_U7_T2_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard component of post-haemorrhage nursing care?

options.A: Restricting all movement for at least two weeks
options.B: Watching for signs of surgical site infection
options.C: Assessing the patient for anxiety and fear
options.D: Monitoring haemoglobin and haematocrit blood levels

explanation: Total immobility is harmful and increases the risk of blood clots; early mobilization is encouraged as soon as the patient is stable. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T2#GNS112_U7_T2_h7)

question: What is the primary underlying problem in all types of shock?

options.A: Inadequate tissue perfusion
options.B: Elevated blood glucose levels
options.C: Excessive carbon dioxide retention
options.D: Severe localized tissue trauma

explanation: Shock fundamentally happens when blood flow is insufficient to supply oxygen and nutrients to the body's tissues and organs. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T3#GNS112_U7_T3_h1)

question: Why does metabolic acidosis happen during prolonged shock?

options.A: Cells switch to anaerobic metabolism and produce lactic acid
options.B: Carbon dioxide dissolves directly into the circulating blood plasma
options.C: The kidneys stop filtering hydrogen ions from the bloodstream
options.D: Excessive oxygen enters the cells and lowers blood pH

explanation: Great job thinking about cellular metabolism! When cells don't get enough oxygen, they switch to backup (anaerobic) energy production. This leaves behind lactic acid as waste, which lowers blood pH and causes acidosis.
