explanation: Releasing the skin only after the needle is out allows the tissue layers to slide back over each other, sealing the needle track completely. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h5)

question: At what angle should a standard intramuscular injection needle be inserted into the skin?

options.A: 90 degrees
options.B: 45 degrees
options.C: 15 degrees
options.D: 60 degrees

explanation: A 90-degree angle ensures the needle penetrates through the subcutaneous fat layer and reaches deep into the muscle tissue. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h6)

question: Why is it important to inject the medication slowly into the muscle tissue?

options.A: Rapid injection causes excessive pressure and localized tissue tearing
options.B: Fast injection neutralizes the pH balance of the solution
options.C: Slow administration eliminates the need for skin antisepsis
options.D: Slow delivery ensures the drug bypasses hepatic metabolism

explanation: Forcing fluid quickly into a confined muscle space creates pressure that stretches tissue fibers, leading to sharp pain and potential localized damage. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h6)

question: Which complication is most likely to occur if an injection is administered too close to the posterior-inferior quadrant of the buttocks?

options.A: Sciatic nerve damage
options.B: Brachial plexus strain
options.C: Radial artery laceration
options.D: Femoral hernia formation

explanation: The sciatic nerve runs through the lower, inner quadrant of the gluteal region, making improper dorsogluteal placement a major risk for nerve injury. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h7)

question: What is the primary reason healthcare workers are instructed NOT to recap used needles after administration?

options.A: Used needles automatically lock and cannot accept a cap
options.B: It significantly increases the risk of accidental needle-stick injuries
options.C: Recapping alters the chemical stability of any remaining fluid
options.D: Standard hospital policy mandates immediate disposal in sharps bins

explanation: Attempting to guide a cap back onto a used needle with one hand often leads to accidental punctures and exposure to bloodborne pathogens. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h7)

question: What critical detail must always be included when documenting an intramuscular injection in a patient chart?

options.A: The room temperature at the time of injection
options.B: The brand name of the syringe manufacturer
options.C: The specific anatomical site used
options.D: The name of the nurse assisting with patient positioning

explanation: Documenting the exact site allows subsequent caregivers to rotate injection sites properly and monitor for local reactions. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h8)

question: Why is post-injection monitoring particularly important after administering a medication via the intramuscular route for the first time?

options.A: To monitor for sudden hypersensitivity or allergic reactions
options.B: To ensure the needle track closes completely without bleeding
options.C: To measure the immediate peak drug concentration in urine
options.D: To confirm the patient can ambulate without muscle cramps

explanation: Because IM absorption is relatively rapid, systemic adverse effects or allergic reactions can manifest quickly, requiring prompt clinical intervention. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h8)

question: What is the primary advantage of intravenous therapy over oral medication administration?

options.A: Eliminating all risk of systemic infection
options.B: Lowering overall cost of treatment
options.C: Extending the duration of drug action
options.D: Achieving immediate systemic bioavailability

explanation: Intravenous delivery bypasses absorption barriers and the digestive tract, placing the substance directly into the bloodstream for rapid effect. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h1)

question: Why does intravenous therapy carry a higher risk of rapid adverse drug reactions than the oral route?

options.A: Intravenous drugs are always administered in much larger doses
options.B: Medications bypass first-pass metabolism and enter circulation instantly
options.C: Veins are more sensitive to chemical irritation than the stomach lining
options.D: The kidneys are unable to filter intravenous drugs effectively

explanation: Because the drug reaches target organs without metabolic modification or absorption delays, toxic levels can manifest immediately if a dosing error occurs. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which clinical scenario represents a clear indication for intravenous fluid therapy?

options.A: Routine outpatient vaccination for tetanus
options.B: Asymptomatic mild hypertension in a pregnant woman
options.C: Severe dehydration due to acute gastroenteritis
options.D: Mild tension headache responsive to oral analgesics

explanation: Fluid volume deficits that compromise hemodynamic stability require rapid replacement via the intravenous route. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h2)

question: A patient requires IV fluid resuscitation, but both arms exhibit extensive second-degree burn injuries. What is the appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Cannulate directly through the burned tissue to save time
options.B: Administer all fluids subcutaneously instead of intravenously
options.C: Select an alternative uncompromised site such as a lower extremity or central access
options.D: Refuse the order and wait until the skin heals completely

explanation: Skin integrity over a venipuncture site must be intact to prevent introducing pathogens directly into the bloodstream through damaged tissue. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of applying a tourniquet prior to peripheral cannulation?

options.A: To engorge superficial veins by obstructing venous return
options.B: To numb the skin and reduce insertion pain
options.C: To sterilize the puncture site before cleaning
options.D: To completely stop arterial blood flow to the limb

explanation: A tourniquet impedes venous return toward the heart, causing blood to pool in the distal veins and making them more visible and palpable. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h3)

question: Why is priming the infusion tubing to remove all air bubbles an essential step before connecting it to a patient?

options.A: To activate the chemical composition of the intravenous fluid
options.B: To prevent the introduction of an air embolus into the venous circulation
options.C: To prevent the plastic tubing from collapsing under pressure
options.D: To ensure the fluid flows at a faster rate once opened

explanation: Air entering the bloodstream can travel to the pulmonary or cerebral circulation, resulting in a life-threatening blockage known as an air embolism. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h3)

question: Which vein is commonly located in the antecubital fossa and is frequently chosen for initial venipuncture due to its large size?

options.A: Greater saphenous vein
options.B: Femoral artery branch
options.C: Carotid jugular vein
options.D: Median cubital vein

explanation: The median cubital vein is prominent, well-anchored, and easily palpable in the antecubital fossa, making it a reliable choice for access. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h4)

question: When planning venipuncture on an adult patient's arm, what is the recommended directional strategy for selecting injection sites?

options.A: Choose whichever vein looks largest regardless of its anatomical location
options.B: Start distally on the hand and move proximally for subsequent insertions
options.C: Always start in the antecubital fossa and move down to the fingers
options.D: Use only the dominant arm regardless of previous puncture history

explanation: Beginning at the most distal sites preserves proximal venous network options if a site infiltrates or fails later. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h4)

question: At what angle should an intravenous catheter be inserted through the skin during peripheral cannulation?

options.A: 45 to 60 degrees
options.B: 15 to 30 degrees
options.C: Exactly 90 degrees
options.D: 5 to 10 degrees

explanation: An insertion angle of 15 to 30 degrees allows the needle to pierce the skin and enter the underlying vein wall without puncturing through the posterior wall. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h5)

question: What visual indicator confirms that the needle tip has successfully entered the lumen of a peripheral vein during cannulation?

options.A: The immediate disappearance of the tourniquet effect on the skin
options.B: The appearance of dark blood in the catheter's flashback chamber
options.C: A loud clicking sound as the safety mechanism engages
options.D: A sudden drop in the patient's systemic blood pressure

explanation: Vascular pressure pushes blood back into the clear flashback chamber of the cannula assembly once the vessel lumen is breached. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h5)

question: What critical action must a nurse perform before administering any intravenous medication?

options.A: Warm the medication bag in a microwave
options.B: Elevate the patient's legs above heart level
options.C: Flush the line with concentrated heparin solution
options.D: Verify the five rights of medication administration

explanation: Checking the right patient, medication, dose, route, and time prevents medication errors, which have immediate consequences via the IV route. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h6)

question: Why is pushing certain emergency medications too rapidly into a peripheral vein hazardous?

options.A: It can cause severe cardiovascular collapse or acute toxicity
options.B: It triggers immediate coagulation of the blood in the tubing
options.C: It cools the intravenous fluid below safe body temperature
options.D: It immediately destroys the plastic catheter material

explanation: Rapid systemic delivery bypasses normal dilution and metabolic buffering, sending dangerous concentrations directly to vital organs. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h6)

question: How often should an established peripheral intravenous site and dressing typically be assessed by the nurse?

options.A: Only when the patient complains of severe pain
options.B: Once every week during routine ward rounds
options.C: Immediately after the catheter is scheduled for removal
options.D: Regularly during every shift change and before medication administration

explanation: Frequent visual and manual checks catch early signs of infiltration, phlebitis, or dislodgement before they become severe. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h7)

question: What is the primary rationale for replacing continuous infusion tubing every 72 to 96 hours?

options.A: To prevent the plastic tubing from stretching under continuous pressure
options.B: To recalibrate the drop factor of the drip chamber
options.C: To minimize bacterial colonization and subsequent bloodstream infection
options.D: To comply with regulations regarding clear fluid visibility

explanation: Prolonged use of infusion sets increases the risk of microbial growth within the nutrient-rich fluid inside the tubing, leading to catheter-related infections. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h7)

question: Which clinical sign is most characteristic of local phlebitis at an intravenous site?

options.A: Erythema, warmth, and tenderness along the vein pathway
options.B: Profuse active bleeding around the plastic cannula hub
options.C: Sudden severe chest pain accompanied by acute dyspnea
options.D: Cool skin temperature with marked localized pallor

explanation: Phlebitis is an inflammatory process causing localized redness, heat, pain, and sometimes a hardened cord-like vein. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h8)

question: A patient receiving an intravenous infusion suddenly develops respiratory distress, weak rapid pulse, and cyanosis. Air embolism is suspected. What immediate nursing action should be taken?

options.A: Place the patient in a left lateral Trendelenburg position and administer oxygen
options.B: Sit the patient upright in a high Fowler's position to assist lung expansion
options.C: Remove the intravenous catheter and apply a warm wet compress to the arm
options.D: Flush the intravenous line rapidly with normal saline to clear the vessel

explanation: The left lateral Trendelenburg position traps air in the apex of the right ventricle, preventing it from lodging in the pulmonary artery while emergency care is provided. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h8)

question: What critical check must a nurse perform immediately after removing a peripheral intravenous catheter?

options.A: Measure the exact volume of blood remaining inside the hub
options.B: Send the plastic catheter immediately to the pathology laboratory
options.C: Soak the removed catheter in a disinfectant solution
options.D: Inspect the catheter tip to ensure it is intact

explanation: Checking the removed catheter guarantees that no portion of the plastic tip sheared off and embolized into the patient's bloodstream. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h9)

question: Why should the intravenous catheter be withdrawn parallel to the skin surface during discontinuation?

options.A: To prevent mechanical trauma and laceration of the internal vein wall
options.B: To activate the automatic needle safety guard mechanism effectively
options.C: To prevent the adhesive dressing from sticking to the patient's arm hair
options.D: To ensure that all residual blood drains cleanly into the gauze pad

explanation: Pulling straight out at an improper angle can catch the bevel against the interior wall of the blood vessel, causing pain or tearing. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h9)

question: What is the primary legal purpose of documenting intravenous care in a patient's medical record?

options.A: To serve as a personal diary for the nurse working the evening shift
options.B: To provide a permanent, legally binding record of nursing accountability and care
options.C: To ensure the hospital billing department can charge for the plastic supplies used
options.D: To replace the need for verbal handoff communication during shift changes

explanation: Medical records are legal documents that demonstrate whether the nurse met professional standards of care during patient treatment. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h10)

question: A nurse makes two unsuccessful attempts at peripheral cannulation before successfully placing the line on the third try. How should this be documented?

options.A: Write that multiple attempts occurred without specifying the exact number
options.B: Record all three attempts, including the sites used, gauge size, and patient response
options.C: Document only the final successful attempt to keep the nursing notes neat
options.D: Omit mention of the failed attempts to avoid alarming the medical team

explanation: Every insertion attempt must be documented to monitor vein trauma, site selection history, and patient tolerance accurately. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T4#GNS122_U1_T4_h10)

question: What defines the rectal route of drug administration?

options.A: Applying topical ointment directly to the external perianal skin only
options.B: Swallowing liquid medication to be absorbed through the large intestine
options.C: Inserting medication directly into the rectum for local or systemic effects
options.D: Injecting pharmaceutical agents directly into the rectal muscle wall

explanation: The rectal route specifically involves placing a drug formulation into the rectum for mucosal absorption. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T5#GNS122_U1_T5_h1)

question: When is a healthcare provider most likely to choose the rectal route over the oral route?

options.A: When local skin irritation around the perianal area requires rapid protection
options.B: When the patient experiences persistent vomiting and cannot retain oral medications
options.C: When the patient prefers a painless and fast-acting alternative to intravenous lines
options.D: When the medication has a very unpleasant taste that requires masking

explanation: Vomiting prevents the retention and absorption of oral drugs, making the rectal route a reliable alternative. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T5#GNS122_U1_T5_h1)

question: Which clinical condition is an absolute contraindication for rectal medication administration?

options.A: Chronic stable hypertension
options.B: Mild intermittent constipation
options.C: Low-grade pediatric fever
options.D: Recent rectal or bowel surgery

explanation: Inserting foreign objects into a healing surgical site can cause tissue damage or dehiscence. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T5#GNS122_U1_T5_h2)

question: Severe diarrhea prevents effective rectal drug administration because of which physiological factor?

options.A: Enzymatic degradation increases significantly during high fluid states
options.B: Excessive fluid dilutes the drug beyond any therapeutic concentration
options.C: Rapid peristalsis expels the medication before absorption can occur
options.D: Mucosal shedding completely blocks blood vessels in the lower bowel

explanation: High bowel motility causes the expulsion of the suppository or liquid enema before the drug can cross the mucosal membrane. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T5#GNS122_U1_T5_h2)

question: What is a major advantage of the rectal route compared to oral administration?

options.A: It completely eliminates any risk of local tissue irritation
options.B: Absorption is always 100 percent predictable and rapid
options.C: Patients prefer it over all other non-invasive routes
options.D: It partially avoids first-pass hepatic metabolism

explanation: Drugs absorbed in the lower rectum drain into systemic circulation, bypassing the liver initially. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T5#GNS122_U1_T5_h3)

question: What is a primary disadvantage associated with rectal drug absorption?

options.A: First-pass metabolism in the liver is completely doubled
options.B: Gastric acid destroys the active chemical compound
options.C: Absorption rates are often erratic and inconsistent
options.D: Systemic circulation is delayed by several hours

explanation: Presence of stool, mucosal surface area variations, and variable blood flow make rectal absorption unpredictable. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T5#GNS122_U1_T5_h3)

question: What is the physical characteristic of a standard rectal suppository at room temperature?

options.A: Viscous gel that hardens upon contact with the mucosal wall
options.B: Solid, bullet-shaped mass designed to melt at body temperature
options.C: Liquid suspension packaged in a pressurized metal canister
options.D: Dry powder capsule that requires dissolution in sterile water

explanation: Suppositories are solid medications crafted to retain shape until exposed to internal body heat. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T5#GNS122_U1_T5_h4)

question: How do evacuation enemas differ fundamentally from retention enemas?

options.A: Evacuation enemas contain active hormones, whereas retention enemas contain only tap water
options.B: Evacuation enemas stimulate rapid bowel emptying, whereas retention enemas are held for drug absorption
options.C: Evacuation enemas are absorbed systemically, whereas retention enemas only provide mechanical lubrication
options.D: Evacuation enemas are administered warm, whereas retention enemas must be frozen solid

explanation: Evacuation enemas rely on mechanical distention to clear the bowel, while retention enemas stay in place so the drug can act locally or systemically. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T5#GNS122_U1_T5_h4)

question: Which patient position is standard for administering a rectal suppository?

options.A: High Fowler sitting position
options.B: Supine with legs elevated high
options.C: Left lateral Sims position
options.D: Prone flat on the abdomen

explanation: The left lateral Sims position follows the anatomical curve of the lower bowel, facilitating smooth insertion. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T5#GNS122_U1_T5_h5)

question: Why is inspecting the perianal area before administering a rectal medication essential?

options.A: To determine the exact pH level of the lower intestinal mucosa
options.B: To confirm whether the patient has taken any oral medications within the last hour
options.C: To identify hemorrhoids, fissures, or lesions that could cause pain or bleeding during insertion
options.D: To measure the precise length of the rectal canal for correct depth placement

explanation: Visual inspection reveals local contraindications or painful abnormalities that alter how gently the nurse must perform the procedure. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T5#GNS122_U1_T5_h5)

question: How far should a rectal suppository be inserted in an adult patient?

options.A: All the way into the ascending colon
options.B: Precisely 4 inches into the rectum
options.C: About 1 inch past the internal anal sphincter
options.D: Just inside the external skin folds

explanation: Inserting the medication past the internal sphincter ensures it stays in place rather than being expelled. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T5#GNS122_U1_T5_h6)

question: What is the rationale for asking the patient to take slow, deep breaths during suppository insertion?

options.A: It triggers immediate peristalsis to clear the colon before the drug enters
options.B: It increases systemic blood pressure to speed up drug absorption in the brain
options.C: It prevents the medication from dissolving prematurely in the lower rectum
options.D: It relaxes the anal sphincter muscles, easing insertion and reducing discomfort

explanation: Deep breathing promotes muscular relaxation, minimizing involuntary contraction of the anal sphincter against the insertion finger. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T5#GNS122_U1_T5_h6)

question: What immediate action should a nurse take if a patient expels a suppository two minutes after insertion?

options.A: Immediately force a second suppository into the rectum to make up for lost time
options.B: Inspect the expelled item, check the patient, and consult the prescriber regarding a repeat dose
options.C: Administer an oral antidiarrheal medication to prevent further bowel movements
options.D: Document that the full medication dose was successfully absorbed into the bloodstream

explanation: Immediate expulsion means the drug was not absorbed, requiring clinical consultation before administering another dose. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T5#GNS122_U1_T5_h7)

question: Which rare complication can result from excessive stretching of the rectal wall during insertion?

options.A: Severe respiratory depression and apnea
options.B: Vagal nerve stimulation leading to bradycardia
options.C: Sudden spikes in systemic blood pressure
options.D: Complete paralysis of the lower extremities

explanation: The vagus nerve runs close to the rectum, and mechanical stimulation can occasionally slow the heart rate. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T5#GNS122_U1_T5_h7)

question: What key instruction should be given to a patient after inserting a rectal suppository?

options.A: Walk briskly around the hospital room to stimulate rapid absorption
options.B: Drink a full liter of cold water to accelerate bowel motility
options.C: Remain lying down for 15 to 20 minutes to retain the medication
options.D: Immediately strain to check if the suppository dissolved completely

explanation: Remaining recumbent prevents gravity from expelling the melting medication before mucosal absorption occurs. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T5#GNS122_U1_T5_h8)

question: Which elements must be included in the nursing documentation following a rectal medication administration?

options.A: Only the patient's verbal consent and their preferred sleeping position
options.B: The exact manufacturing batch number and the nurse's home address
options.C: A detailed narrative of the patient's personal family medical history
options.D: Medication name, dose, time, patient tolerance, and any local reaction

explanation: Accurate charting requires recording specific drug details alongside clinical observations and patient responses. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T5#GNS122_U1_T5_h8)

question: What is the primary anatomical layer targeted during an intradermal injection?

options.A: The skeletal muscle tissue underlying the fascia
options.B: The outermost cornified layer of the epidermis
options.C: The dermal layer situated just beneath the epidermis
options.D: The subcutaneous adipose tissue layer

explanation: Intradermal injections specifically deposit substances into the dermis, where vascularity is low enough to allow slow absorption for diagnostic reading. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T6#GNS122_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why is the intradermal route preferred for diagnostic allergy testing instead of the intramuscular route?

options.A: Dermal absorption is slow, allowing safe local immune reactions to be observed
options.B: The intramuscular route requires a much larger gauge needle size
options.C: Intramuscular injections cause too much immediate pain in patients
options.D: Muscle tissue destroys diagnostic proteins before a reaction can occur

explanation: The slow absorption rate in the dermis prevents systemic distribution of potential allergens while letting clinicians observe localized hypersensitivity reactions. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T6#GNS122_U1_T6_h1)

question: What is the most common anatomical site chosen for a routine Mantoux tuberculin skin test?

options.A: The upper outer quadrant of the gluteus
options.B: The anterior chest wall below the clavicle
options.C: The volar surface of the forearm
options.D: The vastus lateralis muscle of the thigh

explanation: The inner forearm is favored because it is easily accessible, relatively hairless, and allows clear observation of localized skin changes. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T6#GNS122_U1_T6_h2)

question: A patient has extensive eczema and severe scarring across both forearms. Which nursing action is most appropriate when preparing for a tuberculin skin test?

options.A: Inject directly through the scarred tissue since depth matters more than skin integrity
options.B: Perform the injection subcutaneously in the upper arm as a direct substitute
options.C: Refuse to perform the test until the skin conditions resolve completely
options.D: Select an alternative clear site such as the upper back after clinical consultation

explanation: Damaged or scarred skin interferes with accurate measurement of induration, necessitating a clean alternative site like the upper back. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T6#GNS122_U1_T6_h2)

question: Which needle gauge range is most appropriate for administering an intradermal injection?

options.A: 21 to 23 gauge
options.B: 25 to 27 gauge
options.C: 30 to 32 gauge
options.D: 18 to 20 gauge

explanation: A 25 to 27 gauge needle provides the fine caliber needed to penetrate only the epidermal-dermal boundary with minimal tissue disruption. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T6#GNS122_U1_T6_h3)

question: What is the maximum standard volume typically administered via an intradermal injection?

options.A: 3.0 mL to 5.0 mL
options.B: 1.5 mL to 2.0 mL
options.C: 0.1 mL to 0.2 mL
options.D: 0.5 mL to 1.0 mL

explanation: Intradermal volumes are kept extremely small, typically 0.1 mL, to ensure a discrete bleb forms without stretching or rupturing the dermal tissue. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T6#GNS122_U1_T6_h3)

question: At what specific angle should the needle be inserted during an intradermal injection?

options.A: At a 90-degree angle perpendicular to the skin
options.B: At a 5 to 15-degree angle to the skin
options.C: At a 45-degree angle to the skin surface
options.D: At a 60-degree angle to the skin surface

explanation: A shallow insertion angle of 5 to 15 degrees ensures the needle remains within the thin dermal layer rather than passing into subcutaneous tissue. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T6#GNS122_U1_T6_h4)

question: What visual and tactile indicator confirms that an intradermal medication has been administered correctly?

options.A: Numbness spreading rapidly across the entire forearm surface
options.B: Immediate blanching of a wide area surrounding the injection site
options.C: Immediate bruising and localized bleeding at the puncture site
options.D: A small, pale, raised bubble or bleb forming under the skin

explanation: The formation of a distinct bleb verifies that the fluid has pooled within the tight confines of the dermal layer. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T6#GNS122_U1_T6_h4)

question: What is the standard timeframe within which a Mantoux tuberculin skin test must be read?

options.A: 24 to 36 hours
options.B: 5 to 7 days
options.C: 12 to 24 hours
options.D: 48 to 72 hours

explanation: Delayed-type hypersensitivity reactions peak between 48 and 72 hours, making this the mandatory window for accurate clinical reading. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T6#GNS122_U1_T6_h5)

question: When measuring the result of a tuberculin skin test, what specific characteristic must the nurse evaluate?

options.A: The total diameter of skin redness and surface erythema
options.B: The depth of the remaining injection bleb under the epidermis
options.C: The presence and transverse diameter of palpable induration
options.D: The degree of localized skin pigmentation surrounding the puncture

explanation: Erythema indicates simple vasodilation, but only palpable induration represents the cellular immune response being tested. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T6#GNS122_U1_T6_h5)

question: A nurse administers a tuberculin test, and fluid immediately leaks onto the surface without forming a bleb. What is the correct nursing action?

options.A: Apply a warm compress to force the medication back into the tissue
options.B: Repeat the injection at a new site located several centimeters away
options.C: Wait 48 hours and measure any redness that develops at the site
options.D: Document the test as negative since the fluid was injected

explanation: If the dose fails to enter the dermis, the test is invalid and must be re-administered at a different site. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T6#GNS122_U1_T6_h6)

question: Which emergency medication must always be readily available when performing allergy skin testing?

options.A: Digoxin
options.B: Atropine
options.C: Epinephrine
options.D: Furosemide

explanation: Allergy skin tests introduce known allergens, carrying a small risk of triggering acute anaphylaxis, which requires immediate epinephrine administration. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T6#GNS122_U1_T6_h6)

question: Which detail is NOT required when documenting an intradermal injection in the patient record?

options.A: The specific manufacturer and lot number of the antigen
options.B: The brand of soap the patient used before arriving
options.C: The exact anatomical site used for the injection
options.D: The exact date and time the injection was administered

explanation: Patient hygiene products are clinically irrelevant to the procedure documentation; medication details, site, date, and time are essential. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T6#GNS122_U1_T6_h7)

question: Why is it important to instruct a patient not to scratch or apply ointment to an intradermal injection site prior to the reading?

options.A: Scratching pushes the medication deeper into the muscle tissue
options.B: It prevents localized skin irritation from mimicking or obscuring induration
options.C: Ointments neutralize the antigen before an immune response can start
options.D: Rubbing causes the needle track to open and bleed profusely

explanation: Friction and topical products cause inflammation and redness that interfere with accurate reading of the actual test reaction. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T6#GNS122_U1_T6_h7)

question: What is the primary pharmacological advantage of the subcutaneous route over the intravenous route?

options.A: Allows for the administration of large fluid volumes
options.B: Bypasses first-pass hepatic metabolism entirely
options.C: Provides slower and more sustained drug absorption
options.D: Achieves immediate peak plasma concentrations

explanation: The adipose tissue layer has a sparse vascular supply compared to veins or muscle, which naturally delays drug uptake and prolongs the release profile. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T7#GNS122_U1_T7_h1)

question: Why is subcutaneous tissue well-suited for the administration of basal insulin?

options.A: It has a high concentration of pain receptors that alert the patient to hypoglycemia.
options.B: It provides a stable depot that releases the hormone slowly over many hours.
options.C: It prevents the enzymatic breakdown of peptide hormones by skin flora.
options.D: It contains dense muscular fibers that contract to push insulin into circulation.

explanation: Basal insulin requires a steady, prolonged absorption rate to mimic normal pancreatic output, a feature enabled by the characteristics of fatty tissue. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T7#GNS122_U1_T7_h1)

question: What anatomical layer lies directly beneath the subcutaneous tissue?

options.A: Muscle fascia
options.B: Epidermis
options.C: Dermal papillae
options.D: Periosteum

explanation: The hypodermis is sandwiched between the dermis above and the muscle fascia below, which marks the deepest boundary a subcutaneous needle should reach. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T7#GNS122_U1_T7_h2)

question: How does the vascularity of the hypodermis directly influence medication administration?

options.A: It restricts absorption speed, requiring smaller doses for safety.
options.B: It prevents localized pooling by instantly dispersing fluid via lymphatic drainage.
options.C: It creates a slow absorption depot because capillary blood flow is limited.
options.D: It causes rapid systemic toxicity due to immediate vessel saturation.

explanation: Fewer blood vessels mean drugs diffuse gradually into circulation rather than entering the bloodstream all at once. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T7#GNS122_U1_T7_h2)

question: A patient with diabetes mellitus presents with spongy, thickened skin lumps on both sides of the umbilicus. What phenomenon has most likely occurred?

options.A: Lipohypertrophy due to inadequate site rotation
options.B: Subcutaneous hematoma from hitting a deep arterial vessel
options.C: Localized allergic contact dermatitis from latex exposure
options.D: Fibrotic scarring secondary to repeated intramuscular pricks

explanation: Repeating injections in the exact same spot stimulates fat cell growth and scar tissue formation, creating spongy lumps that erraticize insulin absorption. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T7#GNS122_U1_T7_h3)

question: When administering an injection into the abdominal subcutaneous site, what is the recommended minimum distance to maintain from the umbilicus?

options.A: Half a handbreadth
options.B: Four finger-widths
options.C: One centimeter
options.D: Two inches

explanation: Staying at least two inches away from the umbilicus avoids the highly vascular and sensitive periumbilical tissues. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T7#GNS122_U1_T7_h3)

question: What is the correct sequence when mixing regular (clear) and NPH (cloudy) insulin in a single syringe?

options.A: Draw up the cloudy insulin first, then the clear insulin.
options.B: Inject air into the cloudy vial, draw it up, then draw the clear.
options.C: Mix both vials together in a separate container before extraction.
options.D: Draw up the clear insulin first, then the cloudy insulin.

explanation: Drawing clear before cloudy prevents altering the composition of the short-acting insulin with NPH suspension particles. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T7#GNS122_U1_T7_h4)

question: An adult patient with an average body build requires a routine subcutaneous injection. Which combination of needle gauge and length is most appropriate?

options.A: 19 gauge, 1.5 inches
options.B: 30 gauge, 5/16 inch
options.C: 25 gauge, 5/8 inch
options.D: 21 gauge, 1 inch

explanation: A 25-gauge needle with a 5/8-inch length provides the correct gauge and penetration depth for a standard adult subcutaneous space without crossing into muscle. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T7#GNS122_U1_T7_h4)

question: At what angle should a subcutaneous needle be inserted when using a standard 5/8-inch needle on a patient with moderate adipose tissue?

options.A: 45 degrees
options.B: 90 degrees
options.C: 15 degrees
options.D: 30 degrees

explanation: A 45-degree angle ensures the needle stays within the subcutaneous layer when using longer needles on average body frames. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T7#GNS122_U1_T7_h5)

question: Why is pinching a fold of skin recommended during many subcutaneous injections?

options.A: To squeeze out trapped air bubbles inside the syringe barrel
options.B: To numb cutaneous nerve endings through sustained pressure
options.C: To elevate the adipose layer away from underlying muscle tissue
options.D: To constrict local capillaries and prevent rapid drug dispersion

explanation: Pinching gathers the subcutaneous fat, ensuring the needle enters the correct plane and avoids inadvertent intramuscular deposition. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T7#GNS122_U1_T7_h5)

question: What is the safest practice for handling a needle immediately after administering a subcutaneous injection?

options.A: Place the capped syringe on the bedside table for later disposal.
options.B: Break the needle off the syringe hub before throwing it in the trash.
options.C: Dispose of the unrecapped syringe directly into a rigid sharps container.
options.D: Recap the needle using both hands to ensure it is tightly locked.

explanation: Immediate disposal into a puncture-resistant container without recapping is the primary standard to prevent accidental needlestick injuries. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T7#GNS122_U1_T7_h6)

question: What is the clinical rationale for allowing the skin antiseptic swab to dry completely prior to needle insertion?

options.A: It activates the antimicrobial properties of the alcohol solution.
options.B: It prevents chemical irritation and a stinging sensation as the needle enters.
options.C: It prevents the needle from slipping on wet skin during the quick insertion.
options.D: It ensures the skin remains stretched tightly for better needle penetration.

explanation: Alcohol causes a sharp burning pain if it is dragged into the subcutaneous tissue by the advancing needle point before evaporating. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T7#GNS122_U1_T7_h6)

question: A patient receiving low molecular weight heparin subcutaneously develops a large, firm, painful purple swelling at the injection site. What complication has most likely occurred?

options.A: Allergic contact dermatitis
options.B: Lipohypertrophy
options.C: Intramuscular abscess
options.D: Hematoma formation

explanation: Anticoagulants increase bleeding risk, and trauma from the needle can rupture a small blood vessel, resulting in localized blood pooling under the skin. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T7#GNS122_U1_T7_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a recommended nursing action when monitoring a patient after an anticoagulant injection?

options.A: Educate the patient to report black or tarry stools
options.B: Vigorously massage the injection site to disperse the medication quickly
options.C: Inspect the injection site later for signs of localized bruising
options.D: Monitor the patient for abnormal bleeding or petechiae

explanation: Massaging sites after administering anticoagulants or insulin is contraindicated because it alters absorption rates and can cause trauma, bleeding, or bruising. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T7#GNS122_U1_T7_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing venepuncture?

options.A: Relieving acute pressure within chronically congested lymphatics
options.B: Accessing a vein to draw blood for diagnostic testing
options.C: Measuring arterial blood pressure directly from a vessel
options.D: Delivering high-volume enteral nutrition into the bloodstream

explanation: Venepuncture specifically involves puncturing a peripheral vein to obtain blood specimens for laboratory analysis or therapeutic monitoring. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h1)

question: Why is precision and gentle tissue handling essential during venepuncture?

options.A: It eliminates the absolute need for wearing non-sterile gloves
options.B: It guarantees that the laboratory will process the sample immediately
options.C: It prevents mechanical trauma to the vessel wall and reduces patient pain
options.D: It ensures the vein remains permanently dilated for future procedures

explanation: Gentle technique minimizes vessel damage, decreases the risk of haematoma formation, and improves the overall comfort of the patient. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h1)

question: Which vein located in the antecubital fossa is generally the preferred primary choice for venepuncture?

options.A: Radial artery branch
options.B: Median cubital vein
options.C: Great saphenous vein
options.D: Deep brachial vein

explanation: The median cubital vein is usually large, well-supported by surrounding tissue, and less prone to rolling or bruising. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h2)

question: Why must a clinician exercise extra caution when attempting cannulation of the basilic vein?

options.A: It lacks any valves, causing blood to pool uncontrollably upon entry
options.B: It has thick, rigid walls that completely resist standard needle penetration
options.C: It runs in close anatomical proximity to major nerves and the brachial artery
options.D: It is completely invisible under all lighting conditions without deep ultrasound

explanation: The basilic vein lies near important neural and arterial structures, raising the risk of accidental nerve injury or intra-arterial puncture. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h2)

question: A patient is admitted with a history of left-sided mastectomy and lymph node clearance. Where should the nurse collect a routine blood sample?

options.A: Directly through the surgical scar site on the left chest
options.B: From any suitable superficial vein on the right arm
options.C: From the left antecubital fossa to ensure rapid results
options.D: Any accessible vein on the left arm since years have passed

explanation: Limbs affected by lymph node removal lack proper lymphatic drainage, making them highly susceptible to infection and secondary lymphoedema if punctured. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h3)

question: Which of the following is NOT an acceptable reason to avoid a specific venepuncture site?

options.A: An existing arteriovenous fistula used for renal dialysis
options.B: An area of active inflammation, cellulitis, or open burn
options.C: A large, painful haematoma from a previous failed attempt
options.D: The presence of a strong, regular pulse at the puncture site

explanation: Superstantial veins do not normally pulsate strongly; a pulsing vessel strongly suggests an artery, which is a critical reason to avoid puncture. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h3)

question: What is the primary clinical function of applying a tourniquet prior to venepuncture?

options.A: To obstruct venous return and distend the peripheral veins
options.B: To anchor the deep nerve pathways away from the needle path
options.C: To sterilise the skin surface before the alcohol swab is applied
options.D: To completely halt arterial blood flow to the distal limb

explanation: A tourniquet traps blood in the superficial veins by blocking venous outflow, making them easier to palpate and visualize. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h4)

question: When should used needles and blood collection sharps be disposed of into the designated container?

options.A: After all blood collection tubes have been fully labelled at the desk
options.B: At the end of the entire ward shift during waste collection rounds
options.C: Only after cleaning the workstation and completing patient documentation
options.D: Immediately after withdrawal from the vein, without recapping

explanation: Immediate disposal into a sharps container without recapping prevents accidental needle-stick injuries to healthcare workers. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h4)

question: Why is it clinically critical to allow the skin antiseptic to dry completely before inserting the needle?

options.A: Chemical contact time is required for effective microbial kill and burning sensation prevention
options.B: Drying ensures the vein wall hardens enough to make penetration effortless
options.C: Unflashed alcohol reacts with the evacuated tube additives to destroy red blood cells
options.D: Wet alcohol creates a slippery skin surface that causes the needle to slip sideways

explanation: Antiseptics require adequate drying time to exert their antimicrobial effect; injecting through wet alcohol causes stinging and compromises sterility. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h5)

question: What practice is strictly discouraged because it frequently leads to needlestick injuries?

options.A: Performing thorough hand hygiene
options.B: Recapping used venepuncture needles
options.C: Allowing the antiseptic skin prep to air-dry
options.D: Using single-use disposable gloves

explanation: Attempting to recap a used needle increases the likelihood of missing the cap and puncturing one's own finger. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h5)

question: At what approximate angle should a standard venepuncture needle be inserted into the skin?

options.A: 45 to 60 degrees
options.B: 5 to 10 degrees
options.C: 15 to 30 degrees
options.D: 75 to 90 degrees

explanation: An insertion angle of 15 to 30 degrees allows successful entry into superficial veins while avoiding passing straight through the posterior wall. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h6)

question: Why must the tourniquet be released before or during the final stages of blood collection?

options.A: It permanently damages the arterial wall beneath the applied cuff
options.B: It causes immediate collapse of the patient due to sudden blood pressure drop
options.C: Leaving it tight prevents the evacuated tubes from filling completely
options.D: Prolonged stasis causes haemoconcentration and alters laboratory test results

explanation: Leaving a tourniquet on too long traps fluid and cells, altering parameters like haemoglobin, proteins, and potassium levels. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h6)

question: What immediate action should a nurse take if bright red blood begins pulsing rapidly into the collection tubing?

options.A: Continue filling the tube because bright red blood indicates high oxygenation
options.B: Push the needle deeper into the tissue to secure a more stable anchor
options.C: Tighten the tourniquet further to slow down the high-pressure flow
options.D: Withdraw the needle immediately and apply prolonged direct pressure

explanation: Pulsatile bright red blood indicates accidental arterial puncture, which requires immediate withdrawal and sustained pressure to prevent severe bleeding. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h7)

question: Which complication is characterised by a rapidly swelling, dark area under the skin around the puncture site?

options.A: Haematoma
options.B: Venous thrombosis
options.C: Arteriosclerosis
options.D: Lymphangitis

explanation: A haematoma forms when blood escapes from the punctured vein into the surrounding interstitial tissue, causing localized swelling and bruising. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h7)

question: Why is bending the elbow discouraged after venepuncture in the antecubital fossa?

options.A: It forces venous blood backward into the evacuated collection tube
options.B: It prevents the skin antiseptic from drying completely on the skin
options.C: It permanently damages the median nerve running through the joint
options.D: It places mechanical stress on the puncture site and promotes bruising and haematoma

explanation: Bending the arm creates a pumping action that disrupts the forming platelet plug at the puncture site, leading to subcutaneous bleeding. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h8)

question: When is the correct time to label blood collection specimen tubes?

options.A: At the nurses' station before entering the patient's room
options.B: At the patient's bedside immediately after drawing the blood sample
options.C: After returning from the laboratory following sample drop-off
options.D: At the end of the shift during handover documentation

explanation: Tubes must be labelled at the bedside immediately after collection while still with the patient to prevent misidentification errors. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T8#GNS122_U1_T8_h8)

question: What is the primary advantage of administering medications via the topical route?

options.A: Bypassing the gastrointestinal tract entirely
options.B: Maximizing local drug concentration while minimizing systemic effects
options.C: Achieving high systemic blood concentrations rapidly
options.D: Eliminating the need for patient skin assessments

explanation: Topical medications are designed to act directly on the application site, which delivers a high local dose while keeping the rest of the body largely unexposed. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h1)

question: Why is first-pass metabolism avoided when drugs are administered strictly to the skin?

options.A: The drug enters the dermal capillary bed directly without passing through the liver first
options.B: Skin cells actively destroy the medication before it reaches the bloodstream
options.C: Topical drugs never enter the systemic circulation under any circumstance
options.D: The liver is bypassed because topical agents only affect dead keratin layers

explanation: Drugs absorbed through the skin enter peripheral capillaries and systemic circulation directly, avoiding the portal vein and hepatic first-pass breakdown. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h1)

question: Which topical formulation is best suited for dry, thick, and scaly skin lesions due to its occlusive properties?

options.A: Oil-based ointment
options.B: Transparent gel
options.C: Aqueous lotion
options.D: Water-based cream

explanation: Ointments have a high oil content that traps moisture in the skin, softening thick scales and protecting dry lesions effectively. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h2)

question: A patient presents with a weeping, acute inflammatory skin rash. Which topical vehicle should the nurse expect to be prescribed?

options.A: An alcohol-heavy medicated gel
options.B: A continuous transdermal patch
options.C: A heavy petroleum-based ointment
options.D: A lightweight, non-occlusive cream

explanation: Creams are water-based emulsions that do not trap moisture, making them ideal for weeping lesions where heavy ointments would macerate the tissue. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h2)

question: Which layer of the skin serves as the primary barrier against the penetration of topical medications?

options.A: Subcutaneous adipose layer
options.B: Stratum corneum
options.C: Stratum basale
options.D: Dermal capillary bed

explanation: The stratum corneum is the outermost layer of the epidermis, composed of dead, keratinized cells that tightly resist chemical and drug penetration. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h3)

question: What happens to topical drug absorption when an occlusive dressing is applied over a medicated cream?

options.A: Absorption stops entirely because the medication evaporates
options.B: Absorption decreases because airflow is completely blocked
options.C: Absorption remains unchanged because dressings do not affect skin permeability
options.D: Absorption increases due to skin hydration and trapped body heat

explanation: Occlusive dressings trap moisture and heat, which swells skin cells and vastly enhances the penetration rate of topical active ingredients. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h3)

question: Why is it important to gently clean old medication residue off the skin prior to applying a new dose?

options.A: To eliminate the need for hand hygiene before the procedure
options.B: To prevent chemical interactions and ensure accurate dosing at the target site
options.C: To permanently strip away the stratum corneum barrier
options.D: To stimulate rapid local blood circulation in the dermis

explanation: Removing old residue prevents buildup, avoids drug interactions, and ensures the fresh dose makes direct contact with the affected skin. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h4)

question: A nurse is preparing to apply a prescribed topical corticosteroid to an infected, weeping skin ulcer. What initial action is most critical?

options.A: Assessing the skin condition and checking the specific order against the patient chart
options.B: Applying an airtight plastic wrap over the ulcer immediately
options.C: Scrubbing the ulcer vigorously with an antiseptic brush
options.D: Warming the ointment tube under direct sunlight

explanation: Safety requires verifying the medication order and evaluating the skin status to ensure the treatment is safe for the current tissue condition. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h4)

question: In which direction should a nurse smooth a topical cream onto a patient's hairy forearm?

options.A: Against the direction of hair growth
options.B: In the direction of hair growth
options.C: In a vigorous circular scrubbing motion
options.D: Vertically from wrist to elbow only

explanation: Smoothing medication in the direction of hair growth prevents irritation and inflammation of the hair follicles, known as folliculitis. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h5)

question: A student nurse is about to scoop an ointment from a multi-dose jar for a patient. What action demonstrates correct technique?

options.A: Using a clean wooden spatula or tongue depressor to remove the ointment
options.B: Pouring sterile water directly into the jar to liquefy the contents
options.C: Using a gloved bare finger to scoop out the required amount
options.D: Warming the entire multi-use container in a microwave before use

explanation: Using a clean spatula prevents microbial contamination of the remaining medication inside a multi-dose container. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h5)

question: Which of the following is a common local complication associated with the prolonged misuse of potent topical corticosteroids?

options.A: Skin atrophy and thinning
options.B: Permanent systemic hypertension
options.C: Hypertrophic hair growth
options.D: Gastrointestinal ulceration

explanation: Prolonged use of potent topical steroids breaks down collagen and dermal matrix proteins, leading to visible skin thinning and atrophy. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h6)

question: Why must a nurse wear gloves when applying potent hormonal or nitroglycerin ointments to a patient?

options.A: To prevent the nurse from accidentally absorbing the potent medication through their own skin
options.B: To keep the patient's skin sterile during the application process
options.C: To warm the medication faster before it touches the patient
options.D: To prevent the medication from staining the patient's bed linens

explanation: Potent drugs can easily cross the skin barrier of healthcare workers during application, leading to occupational exposure and unwanted systemic effects. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h6)

question: What key instruction should a nurse give a patient regarding the thickness of topical cream application?

options.A: Mix the cream with petroleum jelly to double the batch size
options.B: Apply a thick, heavy layer so the skin stays moist all day
options.C: Massage the cream aggressively until it completely disappears into the fat layer
options.D: Apply only a thin, even layer as prescribed, because excess does not speed healing

explanation: Skin can only absorb a specific amount of medication at a time; applying excess cream wastes product and increases systemic absorption risks. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h7)

question: A patient is discharged home with a prescription for a potent medicated skin ointment. Which statement by the patient indicates a need for FURTHER teaching?

options.A: I will call the clinic if I develop a severe burning rash where the cream was put.
options.B: I will wrap the treated area tightly in polythene nylon to make it heal twice as fast.
options.C: I will rotate the placement site for my transdermal patches every single time.
options.D: I will wash my hands thoroughly after applying my ointment every time.

explanation: Occlusive wrapping increases systemic absorption and toxicity risks unless specifically ordered by a doctor, making this statement incorrect. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T9#GNS122_U1_T9_h7)

question: What is the primary objective of medical asepsis?

options.A: Destroying viruses through chemical immersion
options.B: Sterilizing all surgical instrumentation
options.C: Reducing the total number of microorganisms
options.D: Eliminating every single bacterial spore

explanation: Medical asepsis focuses on lowering microbial loads to prevent transmission, unlike surgical asepsis which aims for complete elimination. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h1)

question: How should a nurse handle an object when its sterile status is uncertain?

options.A: Use the object only for minor dressing changes
options.B: Inspect the packaging for minor dust particles
options.C: Rinse the item with sterile water before use
options.D: Assume the object is contaminated

explanation: A core principle of aseptic technique dictates that any doubt regarding sterility requires immediate rejection of the item. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h1)

question: Which clinical procedure requires the strict application of surgical asepsis?

options.A: Performing a routine bed bath for an adult
options.B: Feeding a patient via a nasogastric tube
options.C: Inserting an indwelling urinary catheter
options.D: Administering an oral antibiotic suspension

explanation: Catheterization introduces a conduit directly into the sterile urinary bladder, demanding a completely sterile approach. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h2)

question: What is the fundamental difference between clean technique and sterile technique?

options.A: Clean technique requires sterile gloves while sterile technique uses examination gloves
options.B: Clean technique reduces microbial load while sterile technique eliminates all microorganisms
options.C: Clean technique is performed only by doctors while sterile technique belongs to nurses
options.D: Clean technique applies to surgery while sterile technique applies to outpatient wards

explanation: Medical asepsis decreases the number of pathogens, whereas surgical asepsis achieves total microbial eradication. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h2)

question: Which link in the chain of infection is directly interrupted by performing hand hygiene?

options.A: Infectious agent
options.B: Mode of transmission
options.C: Reservoir source
options.D: Susceptible host

explanation: Washing hands removes transient microorganisms, preventing them from traveling between patients or surfaces. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h3)

question: A contaminated dressing tray acting as a breeding ground for bacteria represents which element of the infection chain?

options.A: Portal of entry
options.B: Infectious exit
options.C: Susceptible host
options.D: Reservoir

explanation: A reservoir is any environment where a pathogen can live, grow, and multiply before infecting a host. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h3)

question: When is handwashing with soap and water strictly preferred over alcohol-based rubs?

options.A: When hands are visibly soiled with organic material
options.B: Before entering a general medical outpatient ward
options.C: Immediately after checking a patient's blood pressure
options.D: When touching unsoiled patient chart folders

explanation: Visible dirt and certain spore-forming pathogens require physical friction and washing with soap and water to clear effectively. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h4)

question: A nurse finishes taking vital signs for a patient with intact skin and no visible body fluids. What is the most appropriate initial action?

options.A: Put on sterile gloves before touching the next chart
options.B: Rinse hands under cold running water without soap
options.C: Wash hands rigorously with medicated bar soap
options.D: Perform hand hygiene using an alcohol-based rub

explanation: For routine non-soiled patient contact, alcohol-based hand rubs provide rapid and efficient microbial reduction. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h4)

question: Which item of personal protective equipment must be removed first when undressing after a procedure?

options.A: Goggles
options.B: Mask
options.C: Gloves
options.D: Gown

explanation: Gloves carry the highest concentration of contaminants and are removed first to prevent transferring pathogens to other surfaces. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h5)

question: What is the primary reason for wearing an N95 respirator instead of a standard surgical mask?

options.A: Providing sterile protection during major abdominal surgery
options.B: Filtering tiny airborne droplet nuclei circulating in the air
options.C: Preventing large fluid splashes from arterial blood spurts
options.D: Shielding the wearer from direct contact with intact skin

explanation: Respirators create a tight seal capable of filtering out microscopic airborne pathogens like tuberculosis bacilli. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h5)

question: What width defines the unsterile border around the outer edge of a sterile drape?

options.A: One inch
options.B: Six centimeters
options.C: Three inches
options.D: Half a meter

explanation: Standard protocol dictates that the outer one-inch margin of any sterile field is unsterile due to handling during setup. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h6)

question: Why must a nurse never turn their back on an established sterile field?

options.A: Sterile forceps will automatically slide off the edge of the metal table
options.B: Unobserved areas can become accidentally contaminated without the nurse knowing
options.C: Air currents from the back will blow dust particles onto the sterile supplies
options.D: Hospital regulations require continuous visual supervision of all trays

explanation: Maintaining visual contact ensures that any accidental breach of sterility is immediately noticed and corrected. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h6)

question: How should a nurse manage hand hygiene during unexpected water shortages in a clinic?

options.A: Postpone all direct patient care until municipal water supply returns
options.B: Wear examination gloves continuously without changing between tasks
options.C: Wipe hands clean with standard paper towels without applying liquids
options.D: Use stored water systems like tippy-taps or alcohol-based hand rubs

explanation: Alternative water delivery setups and alcohol rubs maintain infection control standards during municipal supply disruptions. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a direct consequence of healthcare-associated infections?

options.A: Increased financial burden on families
options.B: Decreased overall length of hospital stay
options.C: Prolonged recovery periods for patients
options.D: Elevated risk of patient mortality

explanation: HAIs invariably prolong hospital stays rather than shortening them, making infection prevention vital. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T1#GNS122_U2_T1_h7)

question: What is the main goal of medical asepsis in the ward?

options.A: To kill all bacterial spores
options.B: To replace hand hygiene completely
options.C: To sterilize all medical instruments
options.D: To reduce the number of germs

explanation: Medical asepsis is all about cutting down the number of germs and stopping them from spreading. Surgical asepsis, on the other hand, aims for complete sterility. You're doing great!

question: When must you clean your hands when wearing gloves?

options.A: Only when the gloves look dirty or torn
options.B: After removing them, but never before
options.C: Before putting them on and after taking them off
options.D: Only before putting on a fresh pair

explanation: Always wash or sanitize your hands before donning gloves and right after doffing them! Gloves can get tiny tears, and your hands can easily pick up germs during removal.

question: Which routine nursing task calls for clean examination gloves?

options.A: Measuring a patient's resting blood pressure
options.B: Handing a clean meal tray to a patient
options.C: Adjusting nasal cannula oxygen flow
options.D: Emptying a urinary catheter drainage bag

explanation: Urine is a body fluid, so you definitely want glove protection to avoid exposure when emptying that drainage bag. Simple and safe!

question: You are about to check the oral temperature of a patient whose skin is intact. What should you do about gloves?

options.A: Skip gloves because skin is intact and no fluids are expected
options.B: Wear standard examination gloves just in case
options.C: Put on sterile surgical gloves
options.D: Wear heavy-duty utility gloves

explanation: For routine checks involving unbroken skin and no body fluids, gloves aren't needed. This saves precious hospital supplies and time!

question: What is a major difference between standard examination gloves and surgical gloves?

options.A: Surgical gloves are strictly sterile and have longer cuffs
options.B: Examination gloves are always thicker and tougher
options.C: Examination gloves come in precise numbered hand sizes
options.D: Surgical gloves are only used for drawing blood

explanation: Surgical gloves are sterile and feature longer cuffs to cover your gown sleeves, keeping the operating field completely germ-free.

question: When should you choose sterile surgical gloves instead of regular exam gloves?

options.A: When performing a procedure inside a sterile body cavity
options.B: During routine physical checks on unbroken skin
options.C: Whenever touching a patient with an infection
options.D: When cleaning up a blood spill on the floor

explanation: Whenever you enter a sterile space or use sterile instruments, you need sterile gloves to keep bacteria out. You've got this!

question: Which glove material gives you a great feel (tactile sensitivity) but can cause nasty allergies?

options.A: Nitrile
options.B: Neoprene
options.C: Vinyl
options.D: Latex

explanation: Natural rubber latex fits like a second skin, but protein allergies make it a risk for both healthcare workers and patients.

question: You need cheap gloves for quick, low-risk tasks where tearing isn't a big worry. Which material is best?

options.A: Latex
options.B: Vinyl
options.C: Surgical
options.D: Nitrile

explanation: Vinyl is budget-friendly and latex-free, making it ideal for quick, low-risk chores where you don't need heavy-duty strength.

question: What is the very first thing you must do before putting on examination gloves?

options.A: Open the outer wrapper
options.B: Perform hand hygiene
options.C: Check the patient's skin
options.D: Wipe down your work table

explanation: Always clean your hands first! Putting gloves on unwashed hands traps germs right against your skin.

question: Why does wearing the correct glove size matter so much in clinical work?

options.A: It prevents tearing and keeps your fingers nimble
options.B: It stops the material from causing latex allergies
options.C: It keeps the gloves completely sterile
options.D: It means you don't have to wash your hands afterwards

explanation: Gloves that are too tight will easily rip, while oversized gloves make it hard to grip things. Finding your right size is key!

question: When taking off dirty gloves, where should your very first move begin?

options.A: Tearing the palm area to loosen a tight fit
options.B: Pulling straight from the fingertips
options.C: Grasping the outside of the cuff and peeling downward
options.D: Snapping the wristband outward with a quick flick

explanation: Pinching the outer cuff lets you peel the glove inside out, trapping all the nasty germs safely on the inside.

question: Why do you hold the first removed glove inside the palm of your remaining gloved hand?

options.A: To stop the latex from releasing powder into the air
options.B: To easily peel off the second glove without touching its dirty outside
options.C: To keep the first glove clean so you can use it again
options.D: To save space in the waste bin

explanation: Ball up the first glove in your palm so your bare fingers can safely slide under the clean inner cuff of the second glove. Clever and safe!

question: Which of these is a dangerous and incorrect practice with disposable medical gloves?

options.A: Cleaning your hands before putting them on
options.B: Choosing nitrile instead of latex
options.C: Washing and reusing them between patients
options.D: Changing them after every single patient

explanation: Disposable gloves are strictly single-use! Washing them ruins their protective barrier and spreads germs around the ward.

question: Which situation is an example of cross-contamination from poor glove habits?

options.A: Not wearing gloves to take a pulse on an arm
options.B: Touching a computer keyboard with gloves you wore during wound care
options.C: Washing your hands right after taking off both gloves
options.D: Choosing a larger glove size to avoid thumb tears

explanation: Using dirty gloves on shared equipment like keyboards transfers patient germs to surfaces where other staff can pick them up.

question: Under standard precautions, when should a nurse wear gloves?

options.A: Whenever you give oral medications to older adults
options.B: Whenever there is a chance of touching blood or body fluids
options.C: During every single interaction with any patient
options.D: Only when caring for patients in isolation rooms

explanation: Standard precautions apply to everyone. If you expect contact with moist body substances, glove up!

question: A patient is in contact precautions for a resistant bug. What is the rule for gloves in this room?

options.A: Wear gloves only if the patient is bleeding
options.B: Keep the same pair on for your whole shift
options.C: Put on gloves before entering the room and remove them before leaving
options.D: Wear gloves only if doing a surgical dressing change

explanation: For contact precautions, put on your gloves right before you step into the room, and take them off before you step out to contain the germs.

question: What is the main difference between a wound dressing and a bandage?

options.A: A dressing is only for bone fractures, and bandages are for skin cuts.
options.B: A bandage absorbs drainage, while a dressing provides structural support.
options.C: A bandage is always sterile, whereas dressings are never sterile.
options.D: A dressing touches the wound directly, while a bandage holds the dressing in place.

explanation: Think of it this way: the dressing is the sweet layer right on the open skin soaking up fluids, while the bandage wraps around it to keep everything secure. You've got this!

question: Why do modern nurses prefer keeping a wound environment moist?

options.A: It leaves the wound completely open to fresh air safely.
options.B: It keeps the body from producing any fluid at all.
options.C: It stops all bacterial growth on the skin completely.
options.D: It lets skin cells repair faster and helps prevent harsh scarring.

explanation: Skin cells love moisture! They glide across a moist wound bed way faster than trying to crawl across a dry, crusty scab. Great nursing knowledge to keep in your pocket.

question: Which type of wound is created under clean, controlled hospital conditions?

options.A: Contaminated laceration
options.B: Traumatic abrasion
options.C: Intentional wound
options.D: Infected ulcer

explanation: An intentional wound is just a planned surgical cut made by a surgeon using strict sterile steps. Nice and straightforward!

question: How do partial-thickness and full-thickness wounds differ in how they heal?

options.A: Partial-thickness wounds heal by skin cell regeneration, while full-thickness wounds need granulation tissue and a scar.
options.B: Full-thickness wounds never form scar tissue like shallow cuts do.
options.C: Partial-thickness wounds go all the way into the muscle layer.
options.D: Partial-thickness wounds always need skin grafts, but full-thickness ones heal on their own.

explanation: When a wound goes deep (full-thickness), the body has to build new tissue from the bottom up to fill the gap before it can close. You're learning clinical anatomy like a pro!

question: Which dressing material comes from seaweed and turns into a soft gel when it meets heavy wound fluid?

options.A: Cotton gauze
options.B: Alginate dressing
options.C: Hydrocolloid pad
options.D: Transparent film

explanation: Alginates are made from seaweed and are superstars at soaking up heavy drainage while forming a comfy gel. Pretty cool nursing trivia!

question: A patient has a deep pressure ulcer on their heel that is draining a lot of fluid. Which dressing is best to handle it?

options.A: Transparent film
options.B: Dry cotton gauze
options.C: Foam dressing
options.D: Paper tape

explanation: Foam dressings are fantastic at cushioning fragile skin while soaking up moderate-to-heavy drainage. Spot on!

question: What do we call wound drainage that is clear and watery?

options.A: Sanguineous
options.B: Fibrinous
options.C: Purulent
options.D: Serous

explanation: Serous fluid comes from plasma—think of the clear liquid you see in a minor blister. Easy terminology to lock down!

question: When should you usually give a patient their pain medication before a scheduled dressing change?

options.A: Right after you finish the dressing change
options.B: About 30 minutes before the procedure
options.C: Only if the patient starts crying
options.D: Two hours before so it wears off

explanation: Giving pain meds about half an hour early gives the drug time to kick in right when you start cleaning sensitive tissue. Patient comfort is key!

question: When you are cleaning a wound, what is the safest direction to wipe?

options.A: From the outer edges inward to the center
options.B: From the cleanest area to the dirtiest area
options.C: In a wild circular motion all over the skin
options.D: From the bottom of the wound straight up

explanation: Always move from clean to dirty! This golden rule stops you from dragging germs from the surrounding skin right back into the open wound.

question: What must you do if an unsterile object accidentally touches your sterile field while setting up?

options.A: Throw away the whole field and set up a fresh sterile kit.
options.B: Spray antiseptic over the area and wait two minutes.
options.C: Wipe the spot with alcohol and keep going.
options.D: Ignore it if the object looked clean enough.

explanation: Safety first! If a sterile field is touched by something unsterile, its clean status is broken and you have to start fresh. Better safe than sorry in infection control.

question: What should you do if an old gauze dressing is stuck tightly to a healing wound?

options.A: Leave the old gauze stuck and put new dressings on top.
options.B: Moisten it gently with sterile normal saline to loosen it.
options.C: Soak the whole patient in hot soapy water.
options.D: Rip it off quickly with a fast jerk to save time.

explanation: Never rip dry gauze off! A little sterile saline softens the dried fluid and protects that precious new skin underneath.

question: Right after finishing a sterile dressing change, what final detail should you write on the dressing tape?

options.A: The hospital's insurance billing code.
options.B: The date, time, and your initials.
options.C: The patient's diagnosis and room number.
options.D: A friendly smiley face for the patient.

explanation: Labeling your work lets the rest of the healthcare team know exactly when the dressing was changed and who did it. Professional habit unlocked!

question: Which of these details do you need to write in your nursing notes after a dressing change?

options.A: Wound size, color, and how much drainage you saw
options.B: The exact financial cost of the gauze packs
options.C: What the patient's family members think about it
options.D: The brand name of soap the patient uses at home

explanation: Documentation must stay clinical and objective so everyone can track whether the wound is actually getting better. You're thinking like a registered nurse!

question: What does healthy pink or red granulation tissue tell you about a wound?

options.A: A severe bacterial infection has taken over the site.
options.B: The wound is healing nicely with new blood vessel growth.
options.C: The tissue is dying and needs immediate surgery.
options.D: The dressing material is causing an allergic reaction.

explanation: Granulation tissue is packed with tiny new blood vessels. Seeing that healthy pink/red color is a huge nursing win!

question: What is the term for a surgical emergency where internal organs pop out through an opened surgical wound?

options.A: Ecchymosis
options.B: Dehiscence
options.C: Evisceration
options.D: Maceration

explanation: Evisceration is a scary medical emergency where organs protrude past the incision line. It needs immediate sterile coverage and a surgeon right away!

question: What is your very first nursing action if an abdominal wound suddenly pops open and organs are exposed?

options.A: Cover the organs with sterile saline-soaked dressings and call the surgeon.
options.B: Use your gloved fingers to push the organs back inside.
options.C: Wrap a tight binder around the belly to squeeze the organs back in.
options.D: Leave the wound completely open to the fresh air.

explanation: Keep those exposed organs moist with sterile saline gauze so they don't dry out while you call for emergency surgical help. Emergency handled like a champ!

question: What is the primary purpose of removing sutures after a wound has healed?

options.A: To restart the bleeding process for better healing
options.B: To prevent foreign body inflammation and scarring
options.C: To measure the exact depth of the subcutaneous tissue
options.D: To allow the application of topical antibiotics

explanation: Leaving thread in the skin too long causes unnecessary local irritation, inflammation, and permanent marks across the scar line. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h1)

question: Why do sutures need to be taken out instead of left inside the body permanently?

options.A: Skin cells will permanently grow over the thread and trap it in bone.
options.B: Non-absorbable threads act as foreign objects that can trigger infection.
options.C: The body will naturally dissolve all types of suture material within a week.
options.D: Permanent synthetic threads interfere with normal skin sensation forever.

explanation: Non-absorbable materials do not break down inside the body and will cause chronic irritation or abscess formation if left indefinitely. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h1)

question: Which body area generally requires the earliest suture removal due to a rich blood supply?

options.A: The lower leg
options.B: The lower back
options.C: The knee joint
options.D: The face

explanation: Facial skin heals very fast because of abundant blood circulation, so sutures are removed early to avoid permanent track marks. [learn more](GNS122_U2_T12#GNS122_U2_T12_h2)

question: A patient had surgery on their knee joint two days ago. When should the nurse expect these sutures to be removed?
